questions.question: What happens to a XAML file when you build a WPF project, and what does `InitializeComponent()` do?
questions.shortAnswer: The markup compiler turns each XAML page into a compiled, pre-tokenized binary form (BAML) that is embedded in the assembly, and generates a partial class (`MainWindow.g.cs`) for the root element. `InitializeComponent()`, which lives in that generated half, loads the compiled XAML, builds the object tree, fills the `x:Name` fields and hooks up the event handlers.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **XAML is objects, not text.** An object element such as `<Button>` creates an instance through the type's
  parameterless constructor; attributes set properties (through type converters or markup extensions) or attach
  event handlers.
- **Markup compilation.** For every XAML file with the `Page` build action, the build parses the XAML once and
  stores a compiled, pre-tokenized representation (BAML), so the app does not parse XML or validate property
  values at startup.
- **Generated partial class.** `x:Class="MyApp.MainWindow"` on the root element tells the compiler which class to
  generate. `obj\...\MainWindow.g.cs` declares `partial class MainWindow`, implements `IComponentConnector` and
  contains one field per `x:Name`. Your `MainWindow.xaml.cs` is the other half of the same class.
- **`InitializeComponent()`** calls `Application.LoadComponent(this, uri)`, which loads the BAML, creates the
  tree, assigns the named fields and connects events. It is guarded so it runs once.
- **Two passes.** XAML that references types defined in the same project is compiled in a second markup pass,
  after the C# code has been compiled.

**Detail**

This is why a control declared as `<TextBox x:Name="txtName"/>` is available as `this.txtName` in
code-behind: the field is declared in the generated file and assigned while `InitializeComponent()` runs. Until
that call, the window has no content and every named field is `null`.

Run-time XAML parsing is a separate path: `XamlReader.Load` turns a XAML string or stream into objects while
the app runs, which is useful for user-customisable UI but slower and without a generated class.
pitfalls: Touching a named element before `InitializeComponent()` runs, or deleting the call — the window is empty and the `x:Name` fields are `null`.
Editing the `*.g.cs` file — it is regenerated on every build.
Renaming the code-behind class or namespace without updating `x:Class` — the two partial halves no longer match and the build fails.
Thinking the XAML text is re-parsed every time a window opens; compiled pages are loaded from BAML.
followUps: What is the difference between the `Page`, `Resource` and `Content` build actions in a WPF project?
How would you load a piece of XAML at run time, and what are the limits of doing so?
Why can code-behind use a control declared with `x:Name` as if it were a field?

questions.question: What is a markup extension in XAML? Name the ones you use most and explain how the `{}` escape works.
questions.shortAnswer: A markup extension is the curly-brace syntax in an attribute value: instead of treating the string as a literal or running it through a type converter, the XAML processor creates a `MarkupExtension` object and uses whatever its `ProvideValue` method returns. The everyday ones are `{Binding}`, `{StaticResource}`, `{DynamicResource}`, `{x:Static}`, `{x:Type}`, `{x:Null}`, `{RelativeSource}` and `{TemplateBinding}`.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **`{` means "evaluate this".** The first token after the brace names the extension class (`Binding`,
  `StaticResource` for `StaticResourceExtension` — the `Extension` suffix is optional).
- **Arguments.** Comma-separated tokens without `=` are constructor arguments; `Name=Value` tokens set
  properties after the parameterless constructor runs. `{Binding Name}` and `{Binding Path=Name}` are the same.
- **XAML-language extensions** (the `x:` namespace, defined in System.Xaml): `x:Type`, `x:Static`, `x:Null`,
  `x:Array`.
- **WPF extensions:** `StaticResource` (looked up once, at load time), `DynamicResource` (a deferred reference,
  re-resolved when the resource changes; target must be a dependency property), `Binding`, `RelativeSource`,
  `TemplateBinding`, plus `ComponentResourceKey` and `ThemeDictionary` for control libraries.
- **Nesting** is evaluated deepest first: `{DynamicResource {x:Static SystemColors.ControlBrushKey}}`.
- **Escape:** a value that must start with a literal `{` is prefixed with `{}` — common with `StringFormat`.

**Detail**

Markup extensions exist because some values cannot be written as a plain string: a reference to an object that
already exists (a resource), a static field, `null`, a `Type`, or a binding expression that is evaluated later.
You can write your own by deriving from `MarkupExtension` and overriding `ProvideValue(IServiceProvider)` — for
example an extension that returns all values of an enum for a `ComboBox`.

code.source:
<!-- constructor argument vs named properties: these two bindings are identical -->
<TextBlock Text="{Binding Name}" />
<TextBlock Text="{Binding Path=Name, Mode=OneWay}" />

<Border Background="{StaticResource AccentBrush}" />
<TextBlock Foreground="{DynamicResource {x:Static SystemColors.HighlightBrushKey}}" />
<Style TargetType="{x:Type Button}" />
<ContentControl Content="{x:Null}" />

<!-- {} escapes the braces so StringFormat receives the literal text "{0} items" -->
<TextBlock Text="{Binding Count, StringFormat={}{0} items}" />

pitfalls: Using `DynamicResource` on a property that is not a dependency property — it only works on dependency property targets.
Forgetting the `{}` escape when a value has to begin with a literal curly brace, so XAML tries to resolve a markup extension named `0`.
Giving a custom markup extension two constructors with the same number of parameters — the XAML processor's choice is undefined and it may throw.
followUps: How would you write a custom markup extension, and when is it a better fit than a value converter?
What is the practical difference between `StaticResource` and `DynamicResource`?
Why is `Binding` a markup extension even though its class name does not end in `Extension`?

questions.question: How does the WPF layout system work? Explain the measure and arrange passes and what makes layout expensive.
questions.shortAnswer: Layout is a recursive, two-pass process driven by each parent panel: in the measure pass every child is asked how much space it wants (`Measure` → `MeasureOverride`, stored in `DesiredSize`), and in the arrange pass the parent gives each child its final rectangle (`Arrange` → `ArrangeOverride`). Any change that affects size or position can re-run the passes over the subtree, so layout cost grows with the number of elements involved.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Layout slot.** Every `FrameworkElement` gets a rectangle (its slot) from its parent; the visible content can
  be smaller than the slot. `LayoutInformation.GetLayoutSlot` shows it.
- **Measure pass.** The parent calls `child.Measure(availableSize)`. `Width`, `Height`, `Margin`, min/max values
  and the style are applied, then `MeasureOverride` computes the size the element wants. The result is stored in
  `DesiredSize`.
- **Arrange pass.** The parent calls `child.Arrange(finalRect)`. `ArrangeOverride` decides the final size, and
  margins and alignment place the element inside its slot.
- **Custom layout** = derive from `Panel` and override `MeasureOverride` (measure every child) and
  `ArrangeOverride` (arrange every child).
- **What re-triggers layout:** changing a dependency property whose metadata has `AffectsMeasure` or
  `AffectsArrange` (for example `Width`, `Margin`), adding or removing children, applying a `LayoutTransform`, or
  calling `UpdateLayout()`.

**Performance tips from the docs**
- Prefer a `RenderTransform` to a `LayoutTransform` when other elements don't need to move — render transforms
  don't invoke layout.
- Don't call `UpdateLayout()` unless you really need a synchronous pass.
- Simple panels are cheaper: a `Canvas` costs less than a `Grid`.
- For long lists use a virtualizing panel so only visible items are measured.

`ActualWidth`/`ActualHeight` are *outputs* of layout. They are 0 before the first pass and can change several
times while layout settles, so read them in `Loaded` or `SizeChanged`, not in a constructor.
pitfalls: Reading `ActualWidth`/`ActualHeight` in a constructor — they are 0 until the first layout pass.
Animating `Width`, `Height` or a `LayoutTransform` for a purely visual effect — every frame re-runs layout; a `RenderTransform` does not.
Calling `UpdateLayout()` "to be safe" — it forces a full recursive pass.
In a custom panel, forgetting to call `Measure` on a child before arranging it — its `DesiredSize` is stale or zero.
followUps: What do the `AffectsMeasure` and `AffectsArrange` metadata flags do?
Why does a `StackPanel` give its children infinite space in the stacking direction, and what problems does that cause?
When would you write a custom `Panel` instead of nesting `Grid`s?

questions.question: What is the difference between the logical tree and the visual tree in WPF, and when does it matter?
questions.shortAnswer: The logical tree is the content you declared (Window → Grid → Button → its content); the visual tree is everything that actually renders, including the elements a control template expands into (the Button's Border, ContentPresenter and so on). Resource lookup uses the logical tree, while rendering, hit testing and most routed event routes follow the visual tree.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Logical tree** = content relationships exposed by properties such as `Children`, `Items` and `Content`.
  It is used for resource lookup (`StaticResource`/`DynamicResource` walk up it, then to `Application` resources
  and the theme), for framework notifications such as `Loaded`, and it is the starting point for property value
  inheritance.
- **Visual tree** = all `Visual`-derived objects, including template parts. It defines what is drawn and
  hit-tested, and routed events mostly travel along it.
- **Example.** In the logical tree a `Button` has one child — its content string. In the visual tree it is
  `Button → Border → ContentPresenter → TextBlock`, as defined by the button's control template.
- **Helpers.** `LogicalTreeHelper` (`GetParent`, `GetChildren`, `FindLogicalNode`) and `VisualTreeHelper`
  (`GetParent`, `GetChildrenCount`, `GetChild`, `HitTest`).
- **Content elements** such as `Run` or `Paragraph` are in the logical tree but not the visual tree; their host
  control adds them to event routes.

**When it matters**

Most app code never walks either tree. It matters when you need a part of a template (a `ScrollViewer` inside a
`ListBox`), when a resource "can't be found" from inside a template, or when an event handler on a parent
receives an event whose `OriginalSource` is a template element you never declared. Code that walks the visual
tree of a built-in control is fragile: a different theme or a consumer's custom template changes the structure.
pitfalls: Walking the visual tree in a constructor — template children don't exist until the template is applied (use `Loaded` or `OnApplyTemplate`).
Hard-coding the internal structure of a built-in control; the theme or a custom template can change it.
Treating `LogicalTreeHelper.GetChildren` as "everything on screen" — it skips template visuals.
followUps: How do you get a named element from inside a control's template in code?
Why does a handler on a `StackPanel` receive `Click` events from buttons inside it?
How does property value inheritance (for example `FontSize`) cross a template boundary?

questions.question: What are routed events? Explain bubbling, tunneling and direct routing, and what `e.Handled` changes.
questions.shortAnswer: A routed event is registered with WPF's event system so it can invoke handlers on many elements along the element tree, not only on the element that raised it. Bubbling events travel from the source up to the root, tunneling (`Preview…`) events travel from the root down to the source, and direct events fire only on the source; setting `e.Handled = true` stops normally registered handlers further along the route from running.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Why they exist:** one handler on a parent can serve many children (`<StackPanel Button.Click="OnAnyClick">`);
  composite content (an image inside a button) doesn't break the button's click; `EventSetter`s and
  `EventTrigger`s require routed events; controls can use class handlers that run before instance handlers.
- **Bubbling:** source first, then each parent up to the root. Most routed events bubble.
- **Tunneling:** root first, then down to the source. These are the `Preview` events.
- **Direct:** only the source, like a CLR event — but still usable by `EventSetter`/`EventTrigger` and class
  handling.
- **Input pairs:** a mouse press raises `PreviewMouseDown` (whole tunnel route) and then `MouseDown` (bubble
  route) with the same event data. Marking the preview handled means the bubbling event is not raised for normal
  handlers.
- **`sender` vs `e.Source`:** `sender` is the element whose handler is running; `e.Source` is the element that
  raised the event, and it stays the same as the event travels.
- **Handled is a protocol, not a hard stop:** handlers added with `AddHandler(evt, handler, handledEventsToo: true)`
  (or an `EventSetter` with `HandledEventsToo="True"`) still run.

**Detail**

A custom routed event is registered with `EventManager.RegisterRoutedEvent` (name, strategy, handler type,
owner) and stored in a `public static readonly RoutedEvent` field, with a CLR event wrapper whose `add`/`remove`
call `AddHandler`/`RemoveHandler` — the same idea as a dependency property's CLR wrapper.

Some composite controls class-handle input events: `ButtonBase` overrides `OnMouseLeftButtonDown`, marks the
event handled and raises `Click`, so a plain `MouseLeftButtonDown` handler above a button never runs. The fixes
are the paired preview event (`PreviewMouseLeftButtonDown` — but don't mark it handled, or `Click` is suppressed
too) or a `handledEventsToo` handler.
pitfalls: Handling `MouseLeftButtonDown` on a `Button` and wondering why it never fires — the button class-handles it to raise `Click`; use `PreviewMouseLeftButtonDown` or `handledEventsToo`.
Marking a `Preview` event handled casually — the paired bubbling event is then not raised, which can break built-in control behaviour.
Confusing `sender` (where your handler is attached) with `e.Source` (where the event came from).
Not setting `Handled` after fully handling an event, so a handler further up the tree runs the same action again.
followUps: What is a class handler, and why does it run before instance handlers?
What is an attached event? Give an example from the input system.
When would you create a custom routed event rather than a plain CLR event?

questions.question: A `ListBox` bound to 100,000 items is slow and uses a lot of memory. How does UI virtualization work, and what commonly turns it off?
questions.shortAnswer: List controls such as `ListBox`, `ListView` and `DataGrid` use a `VirtualizingStackPanel` that only generates item containers for the items in view, so the cost depends on what is visible rather than on the collection size. Virtualization silently stops when the items panel is replaced by a non-virtualizing panel, when the list is given unlimited space (inside a `StackPanel` or an outer `ScrollViewer`), when item-based scrolling is switched off, or when grouping is on without `IsVirtualizingWhenGrouping`.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **What is virtualized:** the *containers* (`ListBoxItem`s and their templates). The data items themselves are
  all still in memory — loading only the visible data is *data* virtualization, which no WPF control provides
  out of the box.
- **On by default** for `ListBox` and `ListView` when their items are data-bound; `TreeView`, `ComboBox` and
  custom `ItemsControl`s must opt in (`VirtualizingStackPanel` as the items panel plus `IsVirtualizing="True"`).
- **Switches (attached properties on `VirtualizingPanel`):** `IsVirtualizing`, `VirtualizationMode="Recycling"`
  (container recycling: reuse containers while scrolling instead of creating and destroying them),
  `IsVirtualizingWhenGrouping`, `ScrollUnit`.
- **What breaks it:**
  - Adding `ListBoxItem` objects directly instead of binding `ItemsSource` to data.
  - Mixing container types (a menu with `Separator`s can't recycle).
  - `ItemsPanel` set to a plain `StackPanel` or `WrapPanel`.
  - The list measured with infinite height — inside a vertical `StackPanel`, a `ScrollViewer`, or a `Grid` row
    sized `Auto`. Give it a bounded size (a `*` row).
  - `ScrollViewer.CanContentScroll="False"` or `IsVirtualizing="False"`. If the goal was smooth scrolling, use
    `VirtualizingPanel.ScrollUnit="Pixel"` instead.
  - Grouping without `VirtualizingPanel.IsVirtualizingWhenGrouping="True"`.
- **Other levers:** keep item templates light, use `ScrollViewer.IsDeferredScrollingEnabled` for very heavy
  rows, and page the data from the database for truly large sets.

**Detail**

With recycling, a container that scrolls out of view is reused for a different item, so anything stored on the
container itself (a value set in code, a selection-like flag) shows up on the wrong row. Keep per-item state in
the bound item and let bindings update the recycled container.

code.source:
<!-- ✅ bounded height (star row) + recycling + virtualization kept on when grouping -->
<Grid>
    <Grid.RowDefinitions>
        <RowDefinition Height="Auto" />
        <RowDefinition Height="*" />
    </Grid.RowDefinitions>
    <ListBox Grid.Row="1"
             ItemsSource="{Binding Orders}"
             VirtualizingPanel.IsVirtualizing="True"
             VirtualizingPanel.VirtualizationMode="Recycling"
             VirtualizingPanel.IsVirtualizingWhenGrouping="True"
             VirtualizingPanel.ScrollUnit="Pixel" />
</Grid>

<!-- ❌ the StackPanel measures the ListBox with infinite height: every item is realized -->
<StackPanel>
    <ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding Orders}" />
</StackPanel>

pitfalls: Wrapping the list in a `StackPanel` or `ScrollViewer` for layout convenience — it disables virtualization without any error.
Replacing `ItemsPanel` with a `WrapPanel` for a tile view of thousands of items — WPF has no built-in virtualizing wrap panel.
Storing state on recycled containers instead of on the data item.
Expecting UI virtualization to reduce the memory used by the data itself.
Binding an `Expander.IsExpanded` (or similar UI state) to the container rather than the item — recycling carries the value to the wrong row.
followUps: What is the difference between UI virtualization and data virtualization?
Why can container recycling show stale values, and how do you avoid it?
How would you measure where a slow WPF screen spends its time?
questions.versionNote: `VirtualizingPanel.IsVirtualizingWhenGrouping` and `VirtualizingPanel.ScrollUnit` first appear in .NET Framework 4.5 and are available in every WPF on .NET release (.NET Core 3.0 onward). Container recycling dates from .NET Framework 3.5 SP1.

questions.question: What is property value inheritance in WPF? Give examples, and explain why a child sometimes does not pick up the parent's value.
questions.shortAnswer: Property value inheritance lets a dependency property set on a parent flow down to every descendant that doesn't have a value of its own, so you set `FlowDirection` or `DataContext` once on a window instead of on every control. It is opt-in per property (the `Inherits` metadata flag), and an inherited value has low precedence: any local value, style, template or binding on the child wins.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Not class inheritance.** It is about the *element tree*: a child asks its nearest parent for the value, and
  the parent may itself have inherited it, all the way up to the root.
- **Opt-in.** Only properties registered with `FrameworkPropertyMetadataOptions.Inherits` behave this way.
  Built-in examples: `FlowDirection`, `AllowDrop`, `DataContext`, and the font properties such as `FontSize`
  and `FontFamily`.
- **Low precedence.** In the precedence list, inheritance sits just above the metadata default. A locally set
  value, a style setter, a template or a binding on the child overrides the inherited value — which is the usual
  answer to "why didn't my child element change?".
- **Custom inheritable properties** should be registered with `RegisterAttached` (and `Inherits`) so the value
  can cross boundaries in the tree, such as a `Brush` or template content; inheritance of non-attached properties
  across such boundaries is undefined. A `Frame` deliberately blocks inheritance.
- **Cost.** Inheritance makes the property system do more work, so only enable it when you need it.

**Why it matters in MVVM**

`DataContext` is the inherited property you use every day: set the window's `DataContext` to a ViewModel and
every `{Binding}` below it resolves against that object, until some element (an `ItemTemplate` row, a
`UserControl`) sets its own `DataContext`.

code.source:
<!-- Set once on the root; every descendant inherits it unless it sets its own value -->
<Window FlowDirection="RightToLeft" FontSize="14"
        DataContext="{Binding Source={StaticResource Locator}, Path=Main}">
    <StackPanel>
        <TextBlock Text="{Binding Title}" />          <!-- inherits FontSize 14 and the DataContext -->
        <TextBlock Text="Small print" FontSize="10" /> <!-- local value wins over the inherited one -->
    </StackPanel>
</Window>

pitfalls: Expecting a parent value to override a child's local value or style — inheritance has lower precedence than both.
Registering a custom inheritable property with `Register` instead of `RegisterAttached` and then seeing it fail to flow through templates or other tree boundaries.
Turning on `Inherits` for properties that don't need it — it costs performance across the whole tree.
followUps: Where does inheritance sit in the dependency property precedence list?
Why does a `DataTemplate` row get a different `DataContext` from the window?
How would you make a custom "theme accent" property flow to all descendants?

questions.question: You set `Background="Red"` on a button and its style's `IsMouseOver` trigger stopped working. Why? Walk through dependency property value precedence.
questions.shortAnswer: A dependency property can receive values from many places at once, and the property system picks the effective value by a fixed precedence. A local value (an attribute in XAML, `SetValue`, or the CLR setter) outranks everything except coercion and animation, so it beats every style setter and style trigger — the trigger still fires, but its value loses.
questions.answer:
**Key points — the precedence list, highest first**
1. Property system **coercion** (`CoerceValueCallback`).
2. **Active animations** (or ones holding their end value).
3. **Local value** — XAML attribute, `SetValue`, the CLR wrapper. A binding or resource reference set on the
   element has this same level.
4. **TemplatedParent template** values (triggers, then setters inside the template that created the element).
5. **Implicit style** (only affects the `Style` property itself).
6. **Style triggers** (in an explicit or implicit style).
7. **Template triggers.**
8. **Style setters.**
9. **Default (theme) style** — its triggers, then its setters.
10. **Inheritance** from the parent element.
11. **Default value** from the property's metadata.

**Applying it to the question**

`Background="Red"` is level 3, the trigger is level 6, so the button stays red even on mouse-over. Move the red
into the style as a `Setter` (level 8) and the trigger (level 6) wins again. The same thing explains why a locally
set `Foreground` stops a disabled button from greying out: the theme style's `IsEnabled` trigger is level 9.

**Related APIs**
- `ClearValue(prop)` removes only the local value; the next source in the list (often the style) takes over — it
  does not necessarily restore the metadata default.
- `SetCurrentValue(prop, value)` changes the effective value *without* creating a local value, so it doesn't
  overwrite a binding and the next trigger action can still change it. Control authors use it when the control
  updates its own properties.
- `DependencyPropertyHelper.GetValueSource(element, prop)` tells you which level produced the current value —
  handy when debugging.
- Setting a local value on a property that holds a binding or `DynamicResource` replaces it, and `ClearValue`
  won't bring it back.

code.source:
<!-- ❌ local value (level 3) beats the style trigger (level 6): always red -->
<Button Content="Save" Background="Red" Style="{StaticResource HoverButton}" />

<!-- ✅ put the base colour in the style as a setter (level 8); the trigger can now win -->
<Style x:Key="HoverButton" TargetType="Button">
    <Setter Property="Background" Value="Red" />
    <Style.Triggers>
        <Trigger Property="IsMouseOver" Value="True">
            <Setter Property="Background" Value="Yellow" />
        </Trigger>
    </Style.Triggers>
</Style>
<!-- Note: the default Button template has its own hard-coded mouse-over look, so a custom
     ControlTemplate that uses {TemplateBinding Background} may be needed to see the colour change. -->

pitfalls: Fixing "my trigger doesn't work" by adding more triggers instead of removing the local value.
Calling `ClearValue` and expecting the metadata default — the style or theme value applies instead.
Setting a property from code on an element whose value comes from a binding, and silently replacing the binding (use `SetCurrentValue` or change the bound source instead).
Forgetting that the default `Button` template has its own mouse-over visuals, so a background trigger can appear not to work even with correct precedence.
followUps: What is the difference between `SetValue` and `SetCurrentValue`?
Why do animations and coercion rank above local values?
How would you find out at run time where a property's current value came from?

questions.question: What is an attached property? How do you define one, and how are attached properties used to add behaviour to existing controls?
questions.shortAnswer: An attached property is a property defined by one class but set on objects of other classes, written as `Owner.Property` in XAML — `Grid.Row`, `DockPanel.Dock` and `Canvas.Top` are the classic examples, where children tell their layout parent how to place them. You define one with `DependencyProperty.RegisterAttached` plus static `Get<Name>`/`Set<Name>` methods, and when you add a property-changed callback it becomes a hook to attach behaviour to any control.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Why they exist:** a child needs to give its *parent* (or a service) information the child's own class
  doesn't define. A `TextBox` has no `Row` property, but `Grid` reads `Grid.Row` from each child during layout.
- **No ordinary wrapper.** Instead of an instance property, the owner provides
  `public static T GetX(DependencyObject target)` and `public static void SetX(DependencyObject target, T value)`.
  XAML calls these; you call them in code (`Grid.SetRow(box, 1)`).
- **Registration:** `public static readonly DependencyProperty XProperty = DependencyProperty.RegisterAttached(...)`,
  following the `<Name>Property` naming convention.
- **The value lives on the target.** If no parent reads it (a `DockPanel.Dock` on an element outside a
  `DockPanel`), nothing happens and nothing throws.
- **The owner class** doesn't need to derive from `DependencyObject` if it only defines the property for others.
- **Inheritance:** inheritable custom properties should be attached properties.

**Attached behaviours**

Because the property-changed callback receives the `DependencyObject` the value was set on, an attached property
can subscribe to that control's events when it is set. That is how you add things such as "select all text on
focus", "bind `PasswordBox` content" or "scroll to the newest item" to existing controls without subclassing them
or writing code-behind in each view.
pitfalls: Naming the accessors anything other than `Get<Name>`/`Set<Name>` — XAML can't find them.
Putting logic in the accessors — like a normal dependency property wrapper, they can be bypassed; use the property-changed callback.
Subscribing to events in a behaviour without unsubscribing when the value turns false (or the element unloads), which can keep elements alive.
Setting an attached property on an element whose parent doesn't read it and expecting an effect.
followUps: How does `Grid` actually read `Grid.Row` from its children?
What is the difference between an attached behaviour and a `Behavior<T>` from Microsoft.Xaml.Behaviors?
Can a property be both a normal dependency property and an attached property?

questions.question: Explain `ValidateValueCallback`, `CoerceValueCallback` and `PropertyChangedCallback`. When does each run, and how would you keep `Value` between `Minimum` and `Maximum`?
questions.shortAnswer: `ValidateValueCallback` is a static check of the raw value, passed to `Register`, that rejects invalid values by making the set throw; `CoerceValueCallback` lives in metadata, sees the instance and adjusts a value before it becomes effective; `PropertyChangedCallback` also lives in metadata and runs after the effective value has changed. A min/max/value trio is the classic case: coerce `Value` against the limits, and in each property's changed callback call `CoerceValue` on the others.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Validate (`ValidateValueCallback`)**
  - Passed once to `DependencyProperty.Register`; it is **not** metadata and can't be overridden by derived
    classes.
  - Receives only the value — no instance — so it can only enforce rules that are true for every object
    (not infinity, a defined enum member).
  - Returning `false` makes the set throw (`ArgumentException`) and the old value stays.
- **Coerce (`CoerceValueCallback`)**
  - Part of metadata, so derived classes can override it.
  - Receives the instance and the proposed value; returns the value to use. Returning
    `DependencyProperty.UnsetValue` rejects the change.
  - The *desired* (uncoerced) value is remembered: if a constraint is later relaxed, the property system moves
    back towards it. `d.CoerceValue(prop)` re-runs coercion on demand.
  - Default values are not coerced.
- **Changed (`PropertyChangedCallback`)**
  - Part of metadata; receives the instance and `DependencyPropertyChangedEventArgs` (`OldValue`, `NewValue`).
  - Runs when the *effective* value changes, whatever the source — XAML, binding, style, animation — which is
    why it, not the CLR setter, is the place for "when this changes, do that".

**Detail**

Range-style controls (`Slider`, `ProgressBar`, anything derived from `RangeBase`) work this way. If `Maximum`
drops below `Value`, `Value` is coerced down; if `Maximum` goes back up, `Value` returns to what the user
originally set.
pitfalls: Trying to validate against another property inside `ValidateValueCallback` — it has no instance; that logic belongs in coercion.
Clamping inside the CLR setter — XAML, bindings and styles call `SetValue` directly and skip it.
Forgetting to call `CoerceValue` on dependent properties when a limit changes, so `Value` stays outside the new range.
Building circular coercion chains between many properties — it works but costs performance and confuses users.
followUps: What does returning `DependencyProperty.UnsetValue` from a coerce callback do?
Why can derived classes override coercion but not validation?
How does coercion interact with a two-way binding on `Value`?

questions.question: Why should the CLR wrapper of a dependency property contain nothing but `GetValue`/`SetValue`? What goes wrong if you put logic in the setter?
questions.shortAnswer: The WPF XAML loader, data binding, styles and animations don't call your CLR property — they call `SetValue` and `GetValue` on the dependency property identifier directly. Any validation, logging or "on changed" code in the setter therefore runs only when C# code uses the property, so it silently misses most real updates; that logic belongs in the property's metadata callbacks.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **The wrapper is a convenience for C#.** The real storage and change tracking is the property system, keyed by
  the `public static readonly DependencyProperty NameProperty` field.
- **XAML bypasses it for speed.** Using the wrapper would need reflection over `PropertyInfo` for every
  attribute; instead the loader finds the `NameProperty` identifier (by naming convention) and calls `SetValue`.
- **Bindings, styles, triggers and animations** also set the effective value through the property system, not
  the wrapper.
- **Where logic goes instead:**
  - "Do something when it changes" → `PropertyChangedCallback`.
  - "Keep it in range / dependent on another property" → `CoerceValueCallback`.
  - "Reject impossible values" → `ValidateValueCallback`.
- **Inside the control,** prefer `SetCurrentValue` when the control changes its own property in response to
  user input: a plain `SetValue` creates a local value that can replace a binding the consumer set.

**Detail**

The naming convention matters for the same reason: the XAML processor expects the identifier for a property
`Abc` to be `AbcProperty`. A mismatched name, or a wrapper whose name differs from the registered name, leads to
confusing errors at load or binding time.
pitfalls: Debugging "my setter breakpoint never hits" — the value is coming from XAML or a binding, which never calls the setter.
Raising `INotifyPropertyChanged` from a dependency property setter — dependency properties already notify bindings; it is redundant and also skipped by XAML.
Naming the identifier field differently from `<PropertyName>Property`.
Using `SetValue` inside the control to react to input and thereby breaking the consumer's binding.
followUps: When should a control use `SetCurrentValue` instead of `SetValue`?
How do you create a read-only dependency property?
Why do ViewModels use `INotifyPropertyChanged` instead of dependency properties?

questions.question: What decides the default `Mode` and `UpdateSourceTrigger` of a binding? Why does a `TextBox` only update its ViewModel property when it loses focus?
questions.shortAnswer: Both defaults come from the *target* dependency property's metadata, not from `Binding` itself. Most properties bind `OneWay` and update the source on `PropertyChanged`, but user-editable properties such as `TextBox.Text` and `CheckBox.IsChecked` bind `TwoWay`, and `TextBox.Text` deliberately uses `LostFocus` so the source isn't updated on every keystroke.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Modes**
  - `OneWay` — source → target; the usual default for display properties.
  - `TwoWay` — both directions; the default for editable properties (`TextBox.Text`, `CheckBox.IsChecked`).
  - `OneTime` — source → target once, when the binding is first evaluated; later property changes are ignored.
  - `OneWayToSource` — target → source only.
- **The default is per property.** It is stored in `FrameworkPropertyMetadata.BindsTwoWayByDefault`; you can
  inspect it with `TextBox.TextProperty.GetMetadata(typeof(TextBox))`.
- **`UpdateSourceTrigger`** only matters for `TwoWay`/`OneWayToSource` bindings:
  - `PropertyChanged` — immediately (the default for most properties).
  - `LostFocus` — when the control loses focus (the default for `TextBox.Text`, so typing isn't pushed
    character by character and the user can fix typos first).
  - `Explicit` — only when code calls `BindingExpression.UpdateSource()`.
- **Source → target updates** need the source to raise change notifications (`INotifyPropertyChanged`), whatever
  the mode.

**Detail**

Set `UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged` on a `TextBox` when the ViewModel must react while the user types (live
search, enabling a Save button). Keep the default for ordinary form fields, or use `Explicit` for "Apply/Cancel"
dialogs where nothing should change until the user confirms.

code.source:
<!-- TwoWay by default, but the source only updates on LostFocus -->
<TextBox Text="{Binding CustomerName}" />

<!-- live search: push every keystroke to the ViewModel -->
<TextBox Text="{Binding SearchText, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}" />

<!-- display-only: OneWay is already the default for TextBlock.Text -->
<TextBlock Text="{Binding StatusMessage}" />

<!-- value read once; later changes are ignored -->
<TextBlock Text="{Binding AppVersion, Mode=OneTime}" />

pitfalls: Expecting `CanExecute` or validation to react while typing in a `TextBox` without `UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged`.
Assuming every binding is two-way — a `TextBlock` or `Label` will never write back.
Using `OneTime` for a value that is loaded asynchronously after the view appears — it shows the initial (often empty) value forever.
Binding to a read-only source property with a `TwoWay` binding — the binding fails at run time.
followUps: How would you find out whether a given dependency property binds two-way by default?
When is `UpdateSourceTrigger=Explicit` the right choice?
What does `Delay` on a binding do, and how does it compare with debouncing in the ViewModel?

questions.question: Why does a ViewModel implement `INotifyPropertyChanged`, and how do you implement it correctly?
questions.shortAnswer: The binding engine can only refresh the UI when the source tells it a property changed; `INotifyPropertyChanged` is that signal — a single `PropertyChanged` event carrying the property name. Implement it with a setter that compares the new value, stores it, and raises the event with the right name (`[CallerMemberName]` or `nameof` avoids typos).
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Without it,** `OneWay`/`TwoWay` bindings read the value once and never see later changes made in code.
- **One event, a name per property.** `PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name))`.
- **`null` or `string.Empty` as the name** means "all properties changed" — useful after reloading a whole object.
- **Only raise when the value really changes,** to avoid needless UI work and feedback loops.
- **Derived properties** (`FullName` built from `FirstName` + `LastName`) need their own notification when an input
  changes.
- **Collections are different:** replacing a list property needs `PropertyChanged`; adding or removing items
  needs `INotifyCollectionChanged` (`ObservableCollection<T>`).
- **Toolkits remove the boilerplate:** CommunityToolkit.Mvvm's `ObservableObject.SetProperty` and
  `[ObservableProperty]` generate the same pattern.

**Detail**

ViewModels use `INotifyPropertyChanged` rather than dependency properties because it is a plain .NET interface:
the class doesn't have to derive from `DependencyObject`, stays free of WPF types and is easy to unit test.
pitfalls: Raising the event with a misspelled string name — the binding silently never updates (`nameof`/`[CallerMemberName]` prevent this).
Forgetting to notify derived or computed properties.
Assigning a new `List<T>` items in place and expecting the UI to see added items — use `ObservableCollection<T>`.
Raising `PropertyChanged` on every set even when the value is unchanged, causing extra work or loops between two bound properties.
followUps: What does raising `PropertyChanged` with an empty string do?
Why do ViewModels not use dependency properties?
How does `[ObservableProperty]` in CommunityToolkit.Mvvm generate this code?

questions.question: A binding can get its source from `DataContext`, `Source`, `ElementName` or `RelativeSource`. When do you use each, and how do you reach the parent ViewModel from inside an `ItemTemplate`?
questions.shortAnswer: By default a binding resolves its path against the element's inherited `DataContext`; `Source` points at a specific object (often a resource), `ElementName` at a named element in the same XAML namescope, and `RelativeSource` at an element found relative to the target — itself, its templated parent, or an ancestor of a given type. Inside an `ItemTemplate` the `DataContext` is the item, so you reach the window's ViewModel with `RelativeSource AncestorType=...` and `Path=DataContext.SomeCommand`.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **`DataContext` (the default):** set once on a window or view; every descendant inherits it unless it sets its
  own. When it changes, all affected bindings are re-evaluated.
- **`Source`:** an explicit object, typically `{StaticResource ...}` or `{x:Static ...}`. Ignores the
  `DataContext`.
- **`ElementName`:** another element by `x:Name`, for UI-to-UI bindings (a `TextBlock` showing a `Slider` value).
  Limited to the same namescope, so it often fails across template boundaries.
- **`RelativeSource`**
  - `Self` — another property of the same element (`Height` bound to `Width`).
  - `TemplatedParent` — inside a `ControlTemplate`; `TemplateBinding` is the lightweight shorthand for it.
  - `FindAncestor` with `AncestorType` (and optional `AncestorLevel`) — climb to the nearest ancestor of a type.
  - `PreviousData` — the previous item in a data-bound list.
- **Only one** of `Source`, `ElementName` and `RelativeSource` may be set on a binding.

**The item-template case**

Each row's `DataContext` is the item (a `Customer`), but the delete command lives on the window's ViewModel.
Climb to an ancestor whose `DataContext` is that ViewModel and pass the row with `CommandParameter="{Binding}"`.

code.source:
<ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding Customers}">
    <ListBox.ItemTemplate>
        <DataTemplate>
            <DockPanel>
                <!-- DataContext here is one Customer -->
                <Button DockPanel.Dock="Right" Content="Delete"
                        Command="{Binding DataContext.DeleteCustomerCommand,
                                  RelativeSource={RelativeSource AncestorType=ListBox}}"
                        CommandParameter="{Binding}" />
                <TextBlock Text="{Binding Name}" />
            </DockPanel>
        </DataTemplate>
    </ListBox.ItemTemplate>
</ListBox>

<!-- UI-to-UI and Self bindings -->
<Slider x:Name="zoom" Minimum="0.5" Maximum="3" />
<TextBlock Text="{Binding Value, ElementName=zoom, StringFormat={}{0:P0}}" />
<Rectangle Width="80" Height="{Binding Width, RelativeSource={RelativeSource Self}}" />

pitfalls: Binding a row button to `{Binding DeleteCommand}` — the row's `DataContext` is the item, which has no such command.
Using `ElementName` inside a `DataTemplate` or `ControlTemplate` to reach an element outside it — different namescope.
Setting both `ElementName` and `RelativeSource` (or `Source`) on one binding — only one source is allowed.
Overwriting a `UserControl`'s own `DataContext` in its constructor, which cuts it off from the parent's ViewModel.
followUps: What is the difference between `TemplateBinding` and `{Binding RelativeSource={RelativeSource TemplatedParent}}`?
Why can a `ContextMenu` or `ToolTip` not find ancestors with `RelativeSource`?
How does `AncestorLevel` work when the same ancestor type is nested?

questions.question: How do value converters work? When do you need `IMultiValueConverter`, and what should a converter return when it can't convert?
questions.shortAnswer: An `IValueConverter` sits inside a binding: `Convert` runs on the way from source to target and `ConvertBack` on the way back, so a `bool` can become a `Visibility` or a decimal a formatted string. A `MultiBinding` with an `IMultiValueConverter` combines several source values into one target value. When conversion isn't possible, return `DependencyProperty.UnsetValue` (use the fallback) or `Binding.DoNothing` (leave the target as is) rather than throwing, because the binding engine doesn't catch converter exceptions.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Signature:** `Convert(value, targetType, parameter, culture)` and `ConvertBack(...)`; `ConverterParameter`
  lets one converter serve several cases; `culture` comes from the binding's `ConverterCulture` or the element's
  language.
- **Return values with meaning:**
  - `DependencyProperty.UnsetValue` — "no value"; the binding uses `FallbackValue`, or the property's default.
  - `Binding.DoNothing` — don't transfer anything and don't fall back.
  - `null` — a real null value.
- **Exceptions are not swallowed:** anything thrown in `Convert` is a run-time error. Handle expected bad input
  by returning `UnsetValue`.
- **`MultiBinding` + `IMultiValueConverter`:** `Convert(object[] values, ...)` receives one value per child
  binding, in order — for example "enable Save when name and email are both filled". Simple cases may only need
  `MultiBinding.StringFormat`.
- **Built-ins first:** `BooleanToVisibilityConverter`, `StringFormat`, `TargetNullValue`.

**Where converters fit in MVVM**

Converters are view logic — formatting, colours, visibility. If the conversion encodes a business rule
("overdue if past due date and unpaid"), expose it as a ViewModel property instead, where it can be unit tested.
pitfalls: Throwing from `Convert` on unexpected input — it surfaces as a run-time error instead of a graceful fallback.
Putting business rules or database calls in converters; they are hard to test and run on the UI thread for every update.
Ignoring the `culture` parameter when parsing or formatting numbers and dates.
Implementing `ConvertBack` by throwing on a two-way binding (for example a `TextBox`) — every edit then fails.
followUps: What is the difference between returning `DependencyProperty.UnsetValue` and `Binding.DoNothing`?
When would you choose a converter over a computed ViewModel property?
How do you pass a parameter to a converter, and why can't `ConverterParameter` be bound?

questions.question: Compare `ValidationRule`, `IDataErrorInfo` and `INotifyDataErrorInfo` for input validation in WPF. Which fits MVVM best?
questions.shortAnswer: A `ValidationRule` lives on the binding in XAML and checks the value during the transfer to the source; `IDataErrorInfo` lets the ViewModel return one error string per property synchronously; `INotifyDataErrorInfo` lets the ViewModel hold several errors per property and raise `ErrorsChanged` at any time, including after async checks. For MVVM, `INotifyDataErrorInfo` is the usual choice because the rules live in testable code and bindings honour it by default from .NET Framework 4.5 on.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **`ValidationRule` (view side)**
  - Subclass it, override `Validate`, add it to `Binding.ValidationRules`.
  - `ValidationStep` decides when it runs: `RawProposedValue`, `ConvertedProposedValue`, `UpdatedValue` or
    `CommittedValue`.
  - Good for format checks that are purely UI concerns ("must be a number").
- **`IDataErrorInfo` (source side, older)**
  - An indexer `this[string columnName]` returns the error text for a property.
  - Enabled with `ValidatesOnDataErrors=True` (adds a `DataErrorValidationRule`). Synchronous, one error per
    property.
- **`INotifyDataErrorInfo` (source side, modern)**
  - `HasErrors`, `GetErrors(propertyName)` and an `ErrorsChanged` event.
  - Several errors per property, entity-level errors, and validation that finishes later (server or database
    checks).
  - `Binding.ValidatesOnNotifyDataErrors` is `true` by default, so bindings pick it up automatically.
- **Exceptions:** `ValidatesOnExceptions=True` (an `ExceptionValidationRule`) turns conversion or setter
  exceptions into validation errors.

**How the binding engine runs it**

On a source update it runs raw-value rules, then the converter, then converted-value rules, sets the source, then
updated-value and committed-value rules — stopping at the first failure. Failures go into the element's
`Validation.Errors`, set `Validation.HasError`, and are shown by `Validation.ErrorTemplate` (a red border by
default).
pitfalls: Forgetting to raise `ErrorsChanged` after updating the error list — the UI never shows or clears the error.
Putting business validation in `ValidationRule`s in XAML, where it can't be reused or unit tested.
Relying on `UpdateSourceTrigger=LostFocus` and wondering why errors appear only after leaving the field.
Disabling the Save command without checking `HasErrors`, so invalid data can still be submitted.
followUps: How would you validate a field asynchronously (for example "user name already taken")?
How do you customise `Validation.ErrorTemplate` to show the message?
What is a `BindingGroup` and when would you use it?
questions.versionNote: `INotifyDataErrorInfo` support in WPF (and `Binding.ValidatesOnNotifyDataErrors`, default `true`) arrived in .NET Framework 4.5; it is available in all WPF on .NET versions. Older .NET Framework code typically uses `IDataErrorInfo`.

questions.question: What is a collection view (`ICollectionView`/`CollectionViewSource`)? How do you filter, sort and group a list without changing the underlying collection?
questions.shortAnswer: WPF never binds an `ItemsControl` straight to your collection — it binds to a collection view layered on top of it, which adds sorting, filtering, grouping and a current-item pointer without modifying the source. Every collection gets a shared default view (`CollectionViewSource.GetDefaultView`), or you can create your own view with a `CollectionViewSource` so two controls can show the same data differently.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Default view:** binding directly to a collection uses its default view, which is shared by every binding to
  that collection — sort it in one place and every bound control is sorted.
- **Your own view:** `new CollectionViewSource { Source = items }` (or one declared in XAML resources) gives an
  independent view.
- **Sort:** `view.SortDescriptions.Add(new SortDescription("Date", ListSortDirection.Descending))`.
- **Filter:** `view.Filter = o => ...` on an `ICollectionView`, or the `Filter` event on a `CollectionViewSource`.
  Call `view.Refresh()` when the filter criteria change.
- **Group:** `view.GroupDescriptions.Add(new PropertyGroupDescription("Category"))`, displayed through
  `GroupStyle`.
- **Current item:** views track `CurrentItem`; `IsSynchronizedWithCurrentItem="True"` keeps a list's selection
  in step with it, and a `/` in a binding path means "current item" (`{Binding Orders/Total}`) — handy for
  master/detail screens.
- **`DataTable`/`DataView` sources** delegate sorting and filtering to the `DataView`, so those settings are
  shared across views of the same data.

**MVVM angle**

Expose an `ICollectionView` (or keep the view inside the ViewModel and expose the filter text) so search and
sorting logic is testable and the XAML just binds. `ObservableCollection<T>` changes still flow through the view.
pitfalls: Changing filter criteria without calling `Refresh()` — the view keeps the old result.
Sorting the default view for one screen and being surprised that another control bound to the same collection is sorted too.
Rebuilding a new filtered `ObservableCollection` on every keystroke instead of filtering a view.
Grouping a large virtualized list without enabling virtualization for grouping.
followUps: What is the difference between the default view and a `CollectionViewSource` you create?
How does `IsSynchronizedWithCurrentItem` help in a master/detail screen?
How would you add live sorting so an item moves when its sort property changes?

questions.question: A binding silently shows nothing. How do you debug WPF binding failures, and how do `FallbackValue` and `TargetNullValue` differ?
questions.shortAnswer: WPF binding failures don't throw — the binding engine writes a message (path not found, type mismatch) to the debug output and leaves the target at its fallback or default value. In Visual Studio, use the XAML Binding Failures window (or the Output window), turn up `PresentationTraceSources.TraceLevel` on one suspicious binding, and inspect the live element and its `DataContext`. `FallbackValue` is shown when the binding can't produce a value at all; `TargetNullValue` is shown when it succeeds but the source value is `null`.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Why it's silent:** paths are resolved by reflection at run time, so a misspelled property or wrong
  `DataContext` still compiles; the failure only appears while the app runs.
- **Where to look**
  - **XAML Binding Failures** window (Visual Studio 2019 16.8+ and 2022: *Debug → Windows → XAML Binding
    Failures*) lists each failure with data-context type, path, target and, on WPF for .NET 5+, a jump to the
    XAML line.
  - **Output window** — the classic `System.Windows.Data Error: 40 : BindingExpression path error ...` text. For
    WPF on .NET Framework, the *WPF Trace Settings → Data Binding* level must not be Off/Critical.
  - **Per-binding tracing:** `diag:PresentationTraceSources.TraceLevel=High` on one binding logs every step
    (source resolution, value transfer, converter calls).
  - **Live Visual Tree / Live Property Explorer** to check the element's actual `DataContext` and property values.
- **Usual causes:** wrong or late `DataContext`, misspelled path, missing `INotifyPropertyChanged`, a
  `DataTemplate` whose `DataContext` is the item, a converter returning the wrong type, a two-way binding to a
  read-only property.
- **`FallbackValue` vs `TargetNullValue`**
  - `FallbackValue` — used when the binding can't return a value (path doesn't resolve, converter returned
    `DependencyProperty.UnsetValue`).
  - `TargetNullValue` — used when the binding works but the source value is `null` ("(not set)").
  - Both make a failure *visible* during debugging; neither fixes it.

code.source:
<Window xmlns:diag="clr-namespace:System.Diagnostics;assembly=WindowsBase" ...>
    <!-- High trace level for this one binding only: every resolution step goes to the Output window -->
    <TextBlock Text="{Binding Customer.Name,
                      diag:PresentationTraceSources.TraceLevel=High}" />

    <!-- binding broken -> "?" ; binding fine but Phone is null -> "(no phone)" -->
    <TextBlock Text="{Binding Customer.Phone,
                      FallbackValue='?',
                      TargetNullValue='(no phone)'}" />
</Window>

pitfalls: Treating an empty control as "no data" without checking the Output or Binding Failures window first.
Leaving `TraceLevel=High` on many bindings — the output volume slows the app and buries the useful message.
Using `FallbackValue` to hide a broken path instead of fixing it.
On WPF for .NET Framework, having the WPF Trace Settings data-binding level set to Off, so the failures window stays empty.
followUps: How would you find which `DataContext` an element inside a template actually has at run time?
What is the difference between a binding *error* and a binding *warning* in the failures window?
How can compiled bindings or design-time data (`d:DataContext`) catch mistakes earlier?

sources.title: XAML data binding diagnostics - Visual Studio (Windows)

questions.versionNote: The XAML Binding Failures window needs Visual Studio 2019 16.8 or later. Navigating from a failure to its XAML line works for WPF on .NET 5+; for WPF on .NET Framework the failures are listed (from debug output) but without navigation, and the WPF Trace Settings level controls whether they appear.

questions.question: Why can't you bind `PasswordBox.Password` in MVVM, and is wrapping it in a `SecureString` a real security measure?
questions.shortAnswer: `PasswordBox.Password` is a plain CLR property — there is no `PasswordProperty` dependency property — so it can't be a binding target; reading it also puts the password in memory as an ordinary string. Common workarounds are passing the `PasswordBox` (or its `SecurePassword`) as a command parameter, or an attached property that syncs on `PasswordChanged`. `SecureString` only narrows the exposure window: Microsoft recommends not using it for new development on .NET, and its contents are encrypted only on Windows.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Not bindable by design.** `PasswordBox` exposes `MaxLengthProperty`, `PasswordCharProperty` and others as
  dependency properties, but not the password. The docs warn that getting `Password` exposes it as plain text and
  point to `SecurePassword` instead.
- **MVVM-friendly options**
  - Let the view hand the password over at the moment of use: the window implements a small interface
    (`IPasswordProvider`) and is passed as the `CommandParameter`, so the ViewModel reads the password only when
    it authenticates and never references `PasswordBox`.
  - An attached property or behaviour that copies the value on `PasswordChanged` (convenient, but the password
    then lives in a ViewModel property).
- **What `SecureString` really gives you**
  - It is pinned, can be cleared with `Dispose`, and on Windows its buffer is encrypted.
  - It is *not* encrypted on non-Windows platforms, and it must be turned back into plain text to be used
    (`Marshal.SecureStringToBSTR`, interop, sending it to an API).
  - Building it from an existing `string` defeats the purpose — the plain string is already in memory.
  - Microsoft's guidance: don't use it for new development on .NET (Core) or when migrating from .NET
    Framework; prefer not holding the password at all (for example OS-level credentials or tokens from an
    identity provider).
- **Practical rule:** keep the password in the control for as short a time as possible, send it straight to the
  authentication call, then clear the box.
pitfalls: Storing the password in a bindable ViewModel string property "for convenience" and keeping it for the lifetime of the screen.
Converting a `string` to a `SecureString` and believing the password is now protected.
Assuming `SecureString` is encrypted on every platform or after it is marshalled for use.
Logging or displaying the bound password value during debugging.
followUps: How would you unit test a login ViewModel that needs a password?
What would you use instead of storing a password, for example Windows authentication or an OAuth device or browser flow?
Why does `PasswordBox` expose `SecurePassword` at all?
questions.versionNote: The "don't use SecureString for new development" guidance applies to .NET (Core) and to code migrated from .NET Framework. On Windows the `SecureString` buffer is encrypted on both .NET Framework and .NET; on other platforms it is not.

questions.question: Why use commands instead of `Click` event handlers in WPF? Which controls can invoke a command?
questions.shortAnswer: A command separates *what* the user asked for from *who* asked: a button, a menu item and a keyboard shortcut can all invoke the same `ICommand`, and the command's `CanExecute` automatically enables or disables every one of them. In MVVM it also moves the action out of code-behind into the ViewModel, where it can be unit tested.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **`ICommand`** has `Execute(parameter)`, `CanExecute(parameter)` and the `CanExecuteChanged` event.
- **Command sources** implement `ICommandSource` (`Command`, `CommandParameter`, `CommandTarget`). In WPF these
  are `ButtonBase` (Button, CheckBox, RadioButton…), `MenuItem`, `Hyperlink` and `InputBinding` (`KeyBinding`,
  `MouseBinding`).
- **Automatic enabled state:** the source listens to `CanExecuteChanged`, calls `CanExecute`, and disables
  itself when it returns `false` — no manual `IsEnabled` juggling.
- **One action, many triggers:** toolbar button, menu item and `Ctrl+S` all bind to `SaveCommand`.
- **Testability:** a test can call `vm.SaveCommand.Execute(null)` without creating any UI.

**When an event handler is still fine**

Pure view behaviour — focusing a control, starting an animation, scrolling — can stay in code-behind or a
behaviour. Controls and events that don't support commands (for example `SelectionChanged`) need a binding to a
ViewModel property or an event-to-command behaviour.

code.source:
<Window.InputBindings>
    <KeyBinding Key="S" Modifiers="Control" Command="{Binding SaveCommand}" />
</Window.InputBindings>

<DockPanel>
    <Menu DockPanel.Dock="Top">
        <MenuItem Header="_File">
            <MenuItem Header="_Save" Command="{Binding SaveCommand}" InputGestureText="Ctrl+S" />
        </MenuItem>
    </Menu>
    <ToolBar DockPanel.Dock="Top">
        <!-- all three sources are disabled together when SaveCommand.CanExecute returns false -->
        <Button Content="Save" Command="{Binding SaveCommand}" />
    </ToolBar>
</DockPanel>

pitfalls: Setting `IsEnabled` by hand on a button that also has a `Command` — the command's `CanExecute` drives the enabled state.
Putting business logic in `Click` handlers, which makes it untestable and impossible to reuse from a menu or shortcut.
Expecting `CanExecute` to be re-queried automatically when ViewModel data changes — your command must raise `CanExecuteChanged`.
Writing `InputGestureText` on a `MenuItem` and expecting it to create the shortcut — it is display text only; you still need a `KeyBinding`.
followUps: How does a button know when to call `CanExecute` again?
What is the difference between a `RelayCommand` and a `RoutedCommand`?
How do you pass the clicked item to a command?

questions.question: How do WPF's built-in `RoutedCommand`s (`ApplicationCommands.Copy`, etc.) work, and how do they differ from a `RelayCommand` in a ViewModel?
questions.shortAnswer: A `RoutedCommand` contains no logic: its `Execute` and `CanExecute` raise routed events (`PreviewExecuted`/`Executed`, `PreviewCanExecute`/`CanExecute`) starting at the command target — by default the element with keyboard focus — and the first `CommandBinding` up the tree that handles that command does the work. A `RelayCommand` holds delegates to ViewModel methods and runs them directly, with no routing, target or `CommandBinding`.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Four concepts:** the *command* (`ApplicationCommands.Paste`), the *source* (`MenuItem`), the *target* (the
  focused `TextBox`) and the *command binding* (which maps the command to handlers).
- **Routing:** the events tunnel and bubble from the target until a `CommandBinding` for that command is found.
  A binding on an *ancestor* of the target is reached; one on a *descendant* is not.
- **Built-in handling:** `TextBox` already has bindings for Cut, Copy and Paste, so
  `<MenuItem Command="Paste"/>` works with no code — and it pastes into whichever text box has focus.
- **Command library:** `ApplicationCommands`, `NavigationCommands`, `MediaCommands`, `EditingCommands`,
  `ComponentCommands`. Many come with default gestures (Copy → Ctrl+C).
- **`CommandTarget`** is honoured only for routed commands; it is ignored for any other `ICommand`.
- **Input gestures:** `KeyBinding`/`MouseBinding` in `InputBindings` turn a key or mouse gesture into a command
  invocation; you can also add gestures to a routed command's `InputGestures`.

**RoutedCommand vs RelayCommand**

| | `RoutedCommand` | `RelayCommand` / `DelegateCommand` |
|---|---|---|
| Logic lives in | `CommandBinding` handlers (usually code-behind or the control) | ViewModel delegates |
| Depends on focus / tree | Yes — target and routing | No |
| Best for | Editing commands that act on the focused control; control libraries | MVVM application actions |

Many apps use both: built-in routed commands for clipboard/edit actions on controls, relay commands for
everything the ViewModel does.

code.source:
<Window.CommandBindings>
    <!-- Handler in code-behind: routed commands need a CommandBinding somewhere up the tree -->
    <CommandBinding Command="ApplicationCommands.Open"
                    Executed="OpenCmdExecuted"
                    CanExecute="OpenCmdCanExecute" />
</Window.CommandBindings>
<Window.InputBindings>
    <KeyBinding Key="O" Modifiers="Control" Command="ApplicationCommands.Open" />
</Window.InputBindings>

<StackPanel>
    <Menu>
        <!-- built-in: TextBox handles Paste itself; the focused TextBox is the target -->
        <MenuItem Command="Paste" />
        <MenuItem Command="ApplicationCommands.Open" />
    </Menu>
    <TextBox />
    <TextBox />
</StackPanel>

pitfalls: Putting the `CommandBinding` on a child of the target — routing goes up from the target, so it is never reached.
A menu or toolbar button that stays disabled because focus is on an element with no binding for that routed command.
Setting `CommandTarget` with a `RelayCommand` and expecting it to do something — it only applies to routed commands.
Trying to bind a routed command's handlers to a ViewModel without a bridge — routed command handlers are routed-event handlers on elements.
followUps: Why do toolbar buttons with routed commands sometimes stay disabled until you click into a text box?
What is `RoutedUICommand` and what does its `Text` add?
How would you expose an application-wide shortcut such as F5 to refresh the current ViewModel?

questions.question: How should an async operation be exposed as a command? What goes wrong with `async void` handlers, and what does CommunityToolkit.Mvvm's `AsyncRelayCommand` add?
questions.shortAnswer: `ICommand.Execute` returns `void`, so a naive `async void` execute method can't be awaited, gives no "is running" state, lets the user start the operation twice and makes exceptions hard to observe and test. An async command wraps a `Task`-returning method: it exposes the running task and an `IsRunning` flag, disables itself while running (unless concurrency is allowed), supports cancellation through a `CancellationToken`, and lets tests `await` the operation.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Problems with `async void`**
  - Callers (including tests) can't await completion or see the result.
  - An exception escapes on the UI synchronization context and typically crashes the app or goes to the global
    handler, far from the code that caused it.
  - Nothing stops a double click from starting a second save while the first is still running.
- **What an async command should provide:** an `ExecuteAsync` that returns a `Task`, `IsRunning`/`ExecutionTask` for
  busy indicators, `CanExecute` = false while running, cancellation, and one place for exception handling.
- **CommunityToolkit.Mvvm**
  - `AsyncRelayCommand` / `AsyncRelayCommand<T>` (`IAsyncRelayCommand`) expose `ExecutionTask`, `IsRunning`,
    `CanBeCanceled`, `IsCancellationRequested` and `Cancel()`.
  - The `[RelayCommand]` generator on a `Task`-returning method produces an `IAsyncRelayCommand` (the `Async`
    suffix is dropped: `SaveAsync` → `SaveCommand`). A `CancellationToken` parameter enables cancellation;
    `IncludeCancelCommand = true` also generates `SaveCancelCommand`.
  - `AllowConcurrentExecutions` defaults to `false`, so the command reports itself disabled while a run is
    pending.
  - Exceptions are awaited and rethrown by default; `FlowExceptionsToTaskScheduler = true` routes them to
    `ExecutionTask` and `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` instead.
- **Toolkit commands don't use `CommandManager`:** when the result of `CanExecute` changes, call
  `NotifyCanExecuteChanged()` (or use `[NotifyCanExecuteChangedFor]` on the property).
pitfalls: `async void` execute methods with no try/catch — one failed request takes down the app.
Allowing concurrent executions for operations that must not overlap (saves, payments).
Forgetting `NotifyCanExecuteChanged` when the data that `CanExecute` depends on changes — the button never re-enables.
Blocking on the command's task with `.Result` or `.Wait()` in UI code, which can deadlock the UI thread.
followUps: How would you show a busy indicator for one command without a separate `IsBusy` property?
How do you unit test a command that calls an async service?
When would you set `FlowExceptionsToTaskScheduler`?

questions.question: A control raises an event you need in the ViewModel (`Loaded`, `SelectionChanged`, `MouseDoubleClick`) but has no `Command` property. How do you handle it without code-behind?
questions.shortAnswer: First check whether a binding is enough — `SelectedItem="{Binding Selected}"` usually replaces `SelectionChanged`. When you really need the event, the standard tool is the Microsoft.Xaml.Behaviors.Wpf package: an `EventTrigger` inside `Interaction.Triggers` listens for the event and an `InvokeCommandAction` calls a ViewModel command, optionally passing the event args. Keyboard and mouse gestures can also use `InputBindings`.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Prefer state over events.** Many "event" needs are really property changes: bind `SelectedItem`,
  `IsExpanded`, `Text` (with `UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged`) and react in the ViewModel setter.
- **XAML Behaviors (`Microsoft.Xaml.Behaviors.Wpf`)**
  - Open-source (MIT) successor of the Blend SDK's `System.Windows.Interactivity`.
  - XAML namespace `http://schemas.microsoft.com/xaml/behaviors`; C# namespace `Microsoft.Xaml.Behaviors`.
  - `EventTrigger EventName="..."` + `InvokeCommandAction Command="..."`; `PassEventArgsToCommand` sends the event
    args (consider an `EventArgsConverter` so the ViewModel doesn't depend on WPF types).
  - The package targets .NET Framework 4.6.2+ and Windows-targeted .NET (8+).
- **Gestures:** `MouseBinding Gesture="LeftDoubleClick"` or `KeyBinding` in `InputBindings` cover double-clicks and
  shortcuts without any package.
- **Code-behind is acceptable** for view-only reactions; MVVM forbids business logic there, not every line of C#.

**Migration note**

Old projects reference `System.Windows.Interactivity` with the `expression/2010/interactivity` namespace. Moving to
the NuGet package means swapping the assembly reference, the xmlns URI and the `using`s — the API is the same.

code.source:
<Window xmlns:b="http://schemas.microsoft.com/xaml/behaviors" ...>
    <b:Interaction.Triggers>
        <!-- load data when the window appears -->
        <b:EventTrigger EventName="Loaded">
            <b:InvokeCommandAction Command="{Binding LoadCommand}" />
        </b:EventTrigger>
    </b:Interaction.Triggers>

    <ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding Customers}"
             SelectedItem="{Binding SelectedCustomer}">   <!-- state: no event needed -->
        <ListBox.InputBindings>
            <!-- gesture without any package -->
            <MouseBinding Gesture="LeftDoubleClick"
                          Command="{Binding OpenCustomerCommand}"
                          CommandParameter="{Binding SelectedCustomer}" />
        </ListBox.InputBindings>
    </ListBox>
</Window>

pitfalls: Reaching for event-to-command when a two-way binding on a property would do.
Passing raw `RoutedEventArgs` into the ViewModel, which couples it to WPF and makes it hard to test.
Mixing the old `System.Windows.Interactivity` namespace with the new package in one project.
Using a `Loaded` trigger for work that must run once — `Loaded` can fire again when an element is re-added to the tree (tabs, virtualized items).
followUps: What is a `Behavior<T>` and how is it different from an attached property behaviour?
How would you run a command when a `TextBox` loses focus?
Why might `Loaded` fire more than once for the same control?

questions.question: What is the difference between `StaticResource` and `DynamicResource`, and how would you build a light/dark theme switch?
questions.shortAnswer: `StaticResource` looks the key up once while the XAML loads and assigns the object; `DynamicResource` creates an expression that is resolved when the value is needed and re-resolved whenever that resource changes. Use static by default (cheaper, predictable), and dynamic for values that change at run time — themes, system colours and fonts, or dictionaries you swap while the app runs.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **StaticResource**
  - Resolved at load time; later changes to the dictionary entry are not seen.
  - No forward references: the resource must be defined earlier in the dictionary (lexically before use).
  - Works on any property, including non-dependency properties.
  - A missing key is an error (at load time, or at run time if the lookup was deferred).
- **DynamicResource**
  - Deferred expression, re-evaluated when the resource changes, the dictionary is modified, or the element is
    re-parented.
  - Target must be a dependency property on a framework element (or a `Freezable` value, or a `Setter` value).
  - A missing key doesn't throw; the property simply gets its value from elsewhere (style, theme, default).
  - Slightly more overhead, so don't use it everywhere "just in case".
- **Lookup order:** the element's own resources → up the logical tree → `Application.Resources` → (dynamic and
  deferred lookups) the active theme → system resources.

**Theme switching**

Put each theme's brushes in its own `ResourceDictionary` with the same keys, reference those keys with
`DynamicResource`, and swap the merged dictionary in `Application.Resources` at run time — every
`DynamicResource` consumer updates. On .NET 9 and later you can also use the built-in Fluent theme and
`ThemeMode` (`Light`, `Dark`, `System`).
pitfalls: Referencing theme brushes with `StaticResource` and wondering why the theme switch changes nothing.
Using `DynamicResource` everywhere — it adds lookup overhead for values that never change.
Referencing a `StaticResource` before it is defined in the same dictionary (forward reference) and getting a load error.
Expecting `DynamicResource` to work on a plain CLR property.
followUps: In what order does WPF search for a resource key?
Why should resources inside a custom control's theme dictionary use `StaticResource`?
What does `x:Shared="False"` do on a resource?
questions.versionNote: The Fluent theme (`PresentationFramework.Fluent`) and the `ThemeMode` property are available in WPF on .NET 9 and later; on .NET Framework and earlier .NET versions you implement light/dark switching yourself by swapping resource dictionaries.

questions.question: What kinds of triggers does WPF have? When do you use a `Trigger`, `DataTrigger`, `MultiTrigger`/`MultiDataTrigger` and `EventTrigger`?
questions.shortAnswer: A `Trigger` reacts to a dependency property of the styled element (`IsMouseOver`, `IsSelected`); a `DataTrigger` reacts to a bound value, usually from the data item or ViewModel; the `Multi` versions require several conditions at once; and an `EventTrigger` runs actions — typically a storyboard — when a routed event occurs. Property and data triggers apply their setters while the condition holds and undo them automatically when it stops being true.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Where they live:** `Style.Triggers`, `ControlTemplate.Triggers`, `DataTemplate.Triggers` (and
  `FrameworkElement.Triggers`, which only accepts `EventTrigger`s).
- **`Trigger`** — condition on a dependency property of the element (or, in a template, of the templated control):
  `<Trigger Property="IsSelected" Value="True">`.
- **`DataTrigger`** — condition on a `Binding`: `<DataTrigger Binding="{Binding Status}" Value="Overdue">`. Ideal in
  `DataTemplate`s and item styles.
- **`MultiTrigger` / `MultiDataTrigger`** — all conditions must be true (logical AND).
- **`EventTrigger`** — `RoutedEvent="Mouse.MouseEnter"` plus `BeginStoryboard`; no setters, and nothing is
  undone automatically.
- **Enter/exit actions:** property and data triggers can also start storyboards through `EnterActions` and
  `ExitActions`.
- **`TargetName`** setters (affecting a named element inside the template) are only valid in the template's own
  triggers (`ControlTemplate.Triggers`, `DataTemplate.Triggers`); triggers that change the control itself can sit
  in the style.
- **Precedence:** style triggers beat style setters, but a local value on the element beats both.

**Alternatives**

A binding with a converter can do the same job as a data trigger (the docs note it is slightly more efficient),
and `VisualStateManager` states (`Normal`, `MouseOver`, `Pressed`, `Disabled`…) are the other way templates
express control states with animations.

code.source:
<Style TargetType="ListBoxItem">
    <Setter Property="Opacity" Value="0.6" />
    <Style.Triggers>
        <!-- element property -->
        <Trigger Property="IsSelected" Value="True">
            <Setter Property="Opacity" Value="1" />
        </Trigger>
        <!-- bound data value -->
        <DataTrigger Binding="{Binding IsOverdue}" Value="True">
            <Setter Property="Foreground" Value="Firebrick" />
        </DataTrigger>
        <!-- AND of two conditions -->
        <MultiTrigger>
            <MultiTrigger.Conditions>
                <Condition Property="IsMouseOver" Value="True" />
                <Condition Property="IsSelected" Value="False" />
            </MultiTrigger.Conditions>
            <Setter Property="Background" Value="#FFF3E0" />
        </MultiTrigger>
        <!-- routed event -> animation -->
        <EventTrigger RoutedEvent="Mouse.MouseEnter">
            <BeginStoryboard>
                <Storyboard>
                    <DoubleAnimation Storyboard.TargetProperty="Opacity" To="1" Duration="0:0:0.2" />
                </Storyboard>
            </BeginStoryboard>
        </EventTrigger>
    </Style.Triggers>
</Style>

pitfalls: Setting the same property locally on the element — the local value outranks every style trigger.
Using a `Trigger` on a ViewModel property — it only sees dependency properties of the element; use a `DataTrigger`.
Expecting an `EventTrigger` animation to revert by itself like a property trigger setter.
Using `TargetName` in a style trigger — named template parts can only be targeted from template triggers.
followUps: How would you express "OR" between two trigger conditions?
When would you choose `VisualStateManager` over triggers?
Why might a background trigger on a default `Button` appear not to work?
