questions.question: What is the difference between an implicit and an explicit style? Why doesn't my implicit `Button` style apply to `MyButton : Button`, and how does `BasedOn` help?
questions.shortAnswer: A style with `TargetType` and no `x:Key` is implicit — its key is the type itself, so it applies automatically to elements of exactly that type in scope; a keyed style applies only where `Style="{StaticResource Key}"` is set. Implicit lookup uses the element's actual type, so a derived `MyButton` doesn't match a `Button` style unless you reference it explicitly or base a `MyButton` style on it with `BasedOn`.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Implicit style:** `<Style TargetType="Button">` — the implicit key is `typeof(Button)`. It applies to every
  `Button` within the resource scope (control, window or `App.xaml`) that doesn't set `Style` itself.
- **Explicit style:** `<Style x:Key="DangerButton" TargetType="Button">` — applied only on request. Setting
  `Style` explicitly *replaces* the implicit style for that element; the two don't merge.
- **Exact type match:** an implicit `Button` style is not applied to `MyButton`, even though it derives from
  `Button`.
- **`BasedOn`** chains styles: `BasedOn="{StaticResource {x:Type Button}}"` extends the implicit style (or a keyed
  one); setters in the derived style override the base ones.
- **Theme (default) styles** are a separate, lower-precedence layer found through `DefaultStyleKey`; your implicit
  style sits on top of it. `OverridesDefaultStyle="True"` drops the theme style entirely, so you must supply a
  template.

**Typical pattern**

Define an implicit base style for consistency, then keyed variations built on it — "every button looks like
this, danger buttons are also red".

code.source:
<Application.Resources>
    <!-- implicit: applies to every Button (but not to subclasses such as MyButton) -->
    <Style TargetType="Button">
        <Setter Property="Padding" Value="12,6" />
        <Setter Property="FontWeight" Value="SemiBold" />
    </Style>

    <!-- explicit, built on the implicit style -->
    <Style x:Key="DangerButton" TargetType="Button" BasedOn="{StaticResource {x:Type Button}}">
        <Setter Property="Background" Value="Firebrick" />
        <Setter Property="Foreground" Value="White" />
    </Style>

    <!-- give the derived type the same look -->
    <Style TargetType="local:MyButton" BasedOn="{StaticResource {x:Type Button}}" />
</Application.Resources>

<!-- usage -->
<Button Content="Save" />
<Button Content="Delete" Style="{StaticResource DangerButton}" />

pitfalls: Setting `Style` on an element and losing the implicit style's setters — use `BasedOn` instead of starting from scratch.
Expecting an implicit style for a base class to style derived controls.
Defining the implicit style below a keyed style that is `BasedOn` it in the same dictionary — `StaticResource` can't make forward references.
Setting `OverridesDefaultStyle="True"` without providing a `Template`, which leaves the control invisible.
followUps: How does a custom control get its default look without any style in the app?
Where should app-wide implicit styles live, and why?
What is the precedence of an implicit style compared with style setters and local values?

questions.question: How does WPF pick a `DataTemplate` automatically using `DataType`, how is that used for ViewModel-first navigation, and when do you need a `DataTemplateSelector`?
questions.shortAnswer: A `DataTemplate` with `DataType` and no `x:Key` gets an implicit key — the type — so whenever an object of that type is shown as content or as an item, WPF uses that template. Bind a `ContentControl`'s `Content` to a `CurrentViewModel` property and register one template per ViewModel type, and the right view appears when the ViewModel changes. Use a `DataTemplateSelector` when the choice depends on the object's data rather than its type.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Implicit data template:** `<DataTemplate DataType="{x:Type vm:CustomerViewModel}">`. Adding an `x:Key`
  overrides the implicit key and the template is no longer applied automatically.
- **Where it applies:** `ContentControl.Content`, `ItemsControl` items, `ContentPresenter`s — anywhere data is
  displayed without an explicit `ContentTemplate`/`ItemTemplate`.
- **Navigation pattern:** `MainViewModel.CurrentViewModel` holds a `HomeViewModel` or `SettingsViewModel`;
  `<ContentControl Content="{Binding CurrentViewModel}"/>` renders the matching view, and the view's
  `DataContext` is that ViewModel automatically. No view references in the ViewModel.
- **`DataTemplateSelector`:** subclass it, override `SelectTemplate(item, container)`, assign it to
  `ItemTemplateSelector` (or `ContentTemplateSelector`). Use it when items of the *same* type need *different*
  structures (a high-priority task gets a completely different layout).
- **Smaller variations** — colour, visibility — are better done with `DataTrigger`s inside one template.
- **Item styling split:** `ItemTemplate` = how the data looks; `ItemContainerStyle` = the `ListBoxItem` around it
  (selection look, margins); `ItemsPanel` = layout of items.
- **Hierarchies:** `HierarchicalDataTemplate` with `ItemsSource` for `TreeView` and `Menu`.

code.source:
<Window.Resources>
    <!-- one template per ViewModel type: no x:Key, so they apply automatically -->
    <DataTemplate DataType="{x:Type vm:HomeViewModel}">
        <views:HomeView />
    </DataTemplate>
    <DataTemplate DataType="{x:Type vm:SettingsViewModel}">
        <views:SettingsView />
    </DataTemplate>

    <local:TaskTemplateSelector x:Key="TaskSelector"
                                Normal="{StaticResource NormalTaskTemplate}"
                                Urgent="{StaticResource UrgentTaskTemplate}" />
</Window.Resources>

<DockPanel>
    <!-- switching CurrentViewModel in MainViewModel swaps the whole view -->
    <ContentControl Content="{Binding CurrentViewModel}" />

    <!-- same item type, different structure chosen by data -->
    <ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding Tasks}" ItemTemplateSelector="{StaticResource TaskSelector}" />
</DockPanel>

<!-- C#:
public class TaskTemplateSelector : DataTemplateSelector
{
    public DataTemplate? Normal { get; set; }
    public DataTemplate? Urgent { get; set; }
    public override DataTemplate? SelectTemplate(object item, DependencyObject container)
        => item is TaskItem { Priority: 1 } ? Urgent : Normal;
} -->

pitfalls: Giving the type-based template an `x:Key` and wondering why it stopped applying.
Using a selector for differences a `DataTrigger` could handle — selectors don't re-run when a property of the item changes.
Creating views in the ViewModel (`new HomeView()`) instead of letting data templates map ViewModels to views.
Putting selection visuals in the `ItemTemplate` instead of the `ItemContainerStyle`.
followUps: How does the view created by an implicit data template get its `DataContext`?
What happens to the old view and ViewModel when `CurrentViewModel` changes?
When would you use a `HierarchicalDataTemplate`?

questions.question: You are building a lookless custom control (derived from `Control`). How does it get its default template, and how should the code talk to elements inside the template?
questions.shortAnswer: The control overrides `DefaultStyleKey` in its static constructor so WPF looks up a default style for its own type in the theme dictionaries — `Themes/Generic.xaml`, located through `[ThemeInfo]` — and that style sets the default `ControlTemplate`. Code should depend on the template as little as possible: expose dependency properties, commands and routed events that the template binds to, and for the few named parts it really needs, document them with `[TemplatePart]`, find them in `OnApplyTemplate`, and keep working if a part is missing.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Why `Control`:** unlike a `UserControl`, a class derived from `Control` lets consumers replace its whole
  `ControlTemplate`, and it can support themes.
- **Default look**
  - Static constructor: `DefaultStyleKeyProperty.OverrideMetadata(typeof(Rating), new FrameworkPropertyMetadata(typeof(Rating)))`.
  - `Themes/Generic.xaml` (the generic theme dictionary) contains `<Style TargetType="local:Rating">` with the
    template; theme-specific files (`Aero.NormalColor.xaml`, …) are optional.
  - `[assembly: ThemeInfo(ResourceDictionaryLocation.None, ResourceDictionaryLocation.SourceAssembly)]` tells WPF
    where the generic dictionary is (the Visual Studio custom-control template adds this).
  - Theme-level resources need `ComponentResourceKey` keys, not plain strings.
- **Talking to the template — preferred order**
  1. Property bindings and `TemplateBinding` (template reads the control's properties).
  2. Triggers / visual states.
  3. Commands the template's buttons invoke.
  4. Named parts as a last resort.
- **Named parts**
  - Declare them: `[TemplatePart(Name = "PART_Track", Type = typeof(FrameworkElement))]` (the built-in `PART_`
    naming convention, as in `ComboBox`'s `PART_Popup`).
  - Override `OnApplyTemplate()`, call `GetTemplateChild("PART_Track")`, unhook handlers from the old part and
    hook the new one — templates can be replaced at run time.
  - Don't throw if a part is missing or of the wrong type; disable the feature that needed it. Designers
    routinely show incomplete templates.
pitfalls: Forgetting the `DefaultStyleKey` override (or the `ThemeInfo` attribute), so the control renders with no template at all.
Throwing from `OnApplyTemplate` when a part is missing — it breaks designers and partial custom templates.
Wiring part events once in the constructor; parts only exist after the template is applied and change when the template changes.
Putting app-specific resources keyed with strings in `Generic.xaml` instead of `ComponentResourceKey`s.
followUps: When is a `UserControl` the better choice than a custom `Control`?
Why do built-in controls such as `ComboBox` declare `PART_` names?
How would you let consumers restyle a part without retemplating the whole control?

questions.question: Is code-behind forbidden in MVVM? What may go in a view's `.xaml.cs` file and what may not?
questions.shortAnswer: No — MVVM forbids *business and presentation logic* in code-behind, not code-behind itself. The view's code-behind may hold pure UI behaviour that is awkward in XAML (focus, animations, scrolling, wiring a dialog's owner), while anything that decides *what* the app does — loading, saving, validation, enabling actions — belongs in the ViewModel, reached through bindings and commands.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Allowed in code-behind**
  - `InitializeComponent()` and setting the `DataContext` (or receiving the ViewModel through the constructor).
  - Visual behaviour hard to express in XAML: moving focus, starting an animation, scrolling to an item,
    drag-and-drop plumbing.
  - Glue to a control that doesn't bind well (`PasswordBox`, a third-party chart), ideally kept thin or moved into
    an attached behaviour.
- **Not allowed**
  - Business rules, data access, calling services.
  - Enabling or disabling controls by hand — bind `IsEnabled` or use `CanExecute`, so state lives in the
    ViewModel.
  - Reading control values to compute something (`txtAmount.Text`) instead of binding to ViewModel properties.
- **Dependency direction:** the view knows the ViewModel; the ViewModel never references the view or view types
  (`Button`, `Window`, `MessageBox`).
- **Why it matters:** logic in code-behind can't be unit tested without a UI and can't be reused when the view is
  redesigned.

**Rule of thumb**

If the code would still make sense with a completely different-looking view (or no view at all, in a unit test),
it belongs in the ViewModel. If it only makes sense for this particular visual layout, code-behind or a behaviour
is fine.
pitfalls: Treating "zero lines of code-behind" as the goal and building convoluted behaviours for simple focus or scrolling.
Toggling `IsEnabled`/`Visibility` from code-behind instead of binding them to ViewModel state.
Letting the ViewModel call `MessageBox.Show` or create windows, which reverses the dependency.
Accessing named controls from the ViewModel through a reference to the view.
followUps: How do you show a dialog without the ViewModel referencing a window?
When is an attached behaviour better than code-behind?
How would you set focus to a field after validation fails, MVVM-style?

questions.question: How do you show a message box, a file picker or another window from a ViewModel without breaking MVVM?
questions.shortAnswer: Put the UI behind an interface the ViewModel depends on — `IDialogService.Confirm(...)`, `IFileDialogService`, `IWindowService.ShowDialog<TViewModel>()` — and implement it in the view layer, registered with DI. The ViewModel asks for an outcome ("did the user confirm?", "which file?") and never touches `MessageBox`, `OpenFileDialog` or `Window`, so tests can substitute a fake that returns canned answers.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Why not call `MessageBox.Show` directly:** it ties the ViewModel to WPF, blocks unit tests on a modal UI, and
  reverses the dependency (the ViewModel should not know about views).
- **Dialog service:** a small interface returning results, e.g. `bool Confirm(string message, string title)`,
  `string? PickFile(string filter)`. The WPF implementation wraps `MessageBox`/`OpenFileDialog` and can set the
  owner window.
- **Window service:** maps ViewModel types to window types (`Dictionary<Type, Type>` or DI registrations),
  creates the window, sets its `DataContext` and calls `ShowDialog()`; the dialog's ViewModel exposes the result.
- **Closing from the ViewModel:** expose a `RequestClose` event or a `DialogResult` property that the view (or the
  window service) observes — never pass the `Window` into the ViewModel.
- **In-window navigation** usually doesn't need windows at all: swap `CurrentViewModel` and let `DataTemplate`s
  pick the view.
- **Messaging alternative:** a request message (CommunityToolkit.Mvvm `RequestMessage<T>`/`AsyncRequestMessage<T>`) can ask "someone" for an answer, but an injected service is more explicit and easier
  to follow.
- **Testing:** inject a fake `IDialogService` that returns `true`/`false` and assert what the ViewModel did.
pitfalls: Calling `MessageBox.Show` inside a command and then being unable to unit test that command.
Passing the `Window` or a control into the ViewModel "just to close it".
Building one giant dialog service with dozens of methods instead of small, focused interfaces.
Forgetting the owner window, so dialogs open behind the main window or on the wrong monitor.
followUps: How would you return data (not just OK/Cancel) from a custom dialog window?
How do you prevent opening the same tool window twice?
When would you use messaging instead of a dialog service?

questions.question: How do you add dependency injection, configuration and logging to a WPF app using the .NET Generic Host?
questions.shortAnswer: Make `App.xaml.cs` the composition root: remove `StartupUri`, build a host in the constructor or `OnStartup` with `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder` (or `CreateDefaultBuilder`), register services, ViewModels and windows, start the host, then resolve `MainWindow` from the container and show it; stop and dispose the host on exit. The host brings `IServiceProvider`, `appsettings.json` configuration, `ILogger` and `IHostedService` background services — the same model as ASP.NET Core.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Composition root:** delete `StartupUri="MainWindow.xaml"` (otherwise WPF creates the window itself, without
  DI) and create the main window from the container in `OnStartup`.
- **What the host provides:** DI, logging, configuration, app lifetime and `IHostedService`s. The default
  builders load `appsettings.json`, `appsettings.{Environment}.json`, environment variables and command-line args,
  and add Console/Debug/EventSource/EventLog logging.
- **Lifetimes for desktop**
  - Singleton: app-wide services (settings, navigation, dialog service, message bus, a shared app state).
  - Transient: windows and most ViewModels (a new instance each time a screen opens).
  - Scoped: there is no request scope in a desktop app — create scopes yourself (`IServiceScopeFactory`) for
    units of work such as an EF Core `DbContext` per operation.
- **Validation:** scope and build-time validation (`ValidateScopes`, `ValidateOnBuild`) are on by default only in
  the `Development` environment; desktop apps usually run as `Production`, so turn them on explicitly
  (`UseDefaultServiceProvider`) if you want missing registrations to fail at startup.
- **Lifecycle:** `StartAsync` starts hosted services (for example an auto-save `BackgroundService`); on exit call
  `StopAsync` so they get the cancellation signal, then dispose the host.
- **Options pattern:** bind configuration sections to classes (`services.Configure<AppSettings>(...)` or
  `AddOptions<T>().Bind(...).ValidateOnStart()`) and inject `IOptions<T>`.
pitfalls: Keeping `StartupUri`, so WPF creates a second `MainWindow` without its dependencies.
Registering a `DbContext` as a singleton in a long-running desktop app — it grows and goes stale; use a scope or a factory per operation.
Resolving services with `App.Current.Services.GetService(...)` everywhere (service locator) instead of constructor injection.
Assuming `ValidateOnBuild` is on — outside the `Development` environment it is off unless you enable it.
Writing `async void OnExit` and awaiting `StopAsync` — the method returns at the first `await`, so WPF can finish shutting down before the host has stopped.
followUps: Why is "scoped" lifetime awkward in a desktop app, and how do you create scopes?
How would you open a second window with its own ViewModel through DI?
How do background services safely update the UI?
questions.versionNote: Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting is a NuGet package that works with WPF on .NET Framework 4.6.2+ and on .NET; on .NET it is the same hosting model as ASP.NET Core and Worker Services. `Host.CreateApplicationBuilder` is the newer, recommended builder; `Host.CreateDefaultBuilder` is the older callback-based one and is still supported.

questions.question: What does CommunityToolkit.Mvvm give you? Explain `ObservableObject`, `[ObservableProperty]` and `[RelayCommand]` and what code they generate.
questions.shortAnswer: CommunityToolkit.Mvvm (the .NET Community MVVM Toolkit) is a platform-agnostic MVVM library: `ObservableObject` implements `INotifyPropertyChanged`/`INotifyPropertyChanging` with `SetProperty`, and Roslyn source generators turn an annotated field into a full notifying property (`[ObservableProperty]`) and an annotated method into an `IRelayCommand` property (`[RelayCommand]`). The class must be `partial` so the generator can add the other half.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Base types:** `ObservableObject` (change notification), `ObservableValidator` (adds `INotifyDataErrorInfo`
  with data-annotation attributes), `ObservableRecipient` (adds messenger registration tied to `IsActive`).
- **`[ObservableProperty]` on a field**
  - `private string? name;` → `public string? Name { get; set; }` that compares, raises `PropertyChanging`/`PropertyChanged`. Field names `name`, `_name` or `m_name` become `Name`.
  - Partial hooks you may implement: `OnNameChanging(value)`, `OnNameChanged(value)` and old/new-value overloads.
  - `[NotifyPropertyChangedFor(nameof(FullName))]` also notifies a computed property.
  - `[NotifyCanExecuteChangedFor(nameof(SaveCommand))]` re-queries a command when the value changes.
  - `[NotifyDataErrorInfo]` (with `ObservableValidator`) validates the property on every set.
- **`[RelayCommand]` on a method**
  - `void Save()` → `IRelayCommand SaveCommand`; a parameter makes it `IRelayCommand<T>`; a `Task`-returning
    method gives `IAsyncRelayCommand` (the `Async` suffix is dropped).
  - `CanExecute = nameof(CanSave)` links a guard method or property.
- **Requirement:** the containing class (and any containing types) must be `partial`, otherwise you get compile
  errors.
- **Why teams use it:** less boilerplate and fewer typo bugs, the same ViewModels work in WPF, WinUI and .NET MAUI,
  and it is Microsoft-maintained.
pitfalls: Forgetting `partial` on the class (or on an enclosing class) — the generator can't add the property and the build fails.
Binding to the field name (`firstName`) instead of the generated property (`FirstName`).
Writing to the backing field directly inside the class, which bypasses notification.
Adding an access modifier to a generated partial hook such as `OnFirstNameChanged` — it must be declared just `partial`.
followUps: How does `[NotifyCanExecuteChangedFor]` replace `CommandManager.InvalidateRequerySuggested()`?
When would you derive from `ObservableValidator` or `ObservableRecipient` instead of `ObservableObject`?
What are the trade-offs of source generators versus hand-written properties?

questions.question: How do event subscriptions cause memory leaks in MVVM apps, and how do weak events and CommunityToolkit's `WeakReferenceMessenger` help?
questions.shortAnswer: `source.Event += handler` stores a strong reference from the source to the listener, so a long-lived source — a singleton service, a static event, a shared app state — keeps every closed window's ViewModel alive until it unsubscribes. Unsubscribe deterministically when a screen closes, or use a weak subscription: the WPF weak event pattern (`WeakEventManager`) or a weak messenger whose recipients can still be garbage collected.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **The leak:** the event's delegate list in the *source* references the *listener*. If the source outlives the
  listener (app-wide service, static event, parent ViewModel), the listener — and the view bound to it — is never
  collected.
- **Typical culprits:** ViewModels subscribing to a singleton's `PropertyChanged` or `CollectionChanged`, static
  events, timers, message buses with strong references, lambdas capturing `this`.
- **Fix 1 — deterministic cleanup:** unsubscribe in a `Cleanup`/`Dispose` called when the window closes
  (window service or `Closed` handler).
- **Fix 2 — WPF weak event pattern:** `PropertyChangedEventManager.AddHandler(source, handler, "")`, the generic
  `WeakEventManager<TSource, TArgs>` (simplest, but uses reflection and is slower), or a custom `WeakEventManager`.
  WPF data binding already uses weak events internally.
- **Fix 3 — messenger choice (CommunityToolkit.Mvvm)**
  - `WeakReferenceMessenger` tracks recipients weakly; unused recipients can be collected even with handlers
    registered (unregistering is still good for performance).
  - `StrongReferenceMessenger` is faster and lighter but every recipient must be unregistered, or it leaks.
  - `ObservableRecipient` registers on `IsActive = true` and unregisters all handlers on `IsActive = false`.
- **The opposite trap:** `CommandManager.RequerySuggested` holds handlers *weakly*, so if nothing else references
  your handler it can be collected and `CanExecute` silently stops updating.
pitfalls: Subscribing a short-lived ViewModel to a singleton's event and never unsubscribing.
Using `StrongReferenceMessenger` (for speed) without unregistering recipients.
Lambda handlers that capture `this` registered on long-lived sources — they are just as strong as method handlers.
Relying on weak events to *control* behaviour — a listener that is no longer referenced may still receive events until the GC runs.
followUps: How would you prove a window is leaking (memory profiler, `WeakReference` test)?
Why does WPF data binding not usually leak a bound ViewModel?
What is the difference between `Unregister<T>` and `UnregisterAll`?

questions.question: How do you design ViewModels so they can be unit tested, and what would you test?
questions.shortAnswer: A testable ViewModel has no references to views, controls, `Application.Current` or the `Dispatcher`; everything it needs — data services, dialogs, navigation, time, UI-thread marshalling — comes in through constructor-injected interfaces that tests replace with fakes. Then you test it like any class: arrange fakes, execute commands or set properties, and assert on resulting state, raised `PropertyChanged` events, `CanExecute` and calls to the fakes.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Design rules**
  - No WPF types in the ViewModel (`Window`, `MessageBox`, `Brush`, `Visibility`) — expose state such as `IsBusy`
    and let the view convert it.
  - Inject services as interfaces (`IOrderService`, `IDialogService`, `INavigationService`).
  - Make async work return `Task` (async commands expose `ExecuteAsync`), so tests can `await` it.
  - Don't call `Application.Current.Dispatcher` inside ViewModels; if you need marshalling, inject an abstraction
    or rely on `await` resuming on the caller's context.
  - Keep constructors cheap; do loading in an explicit `InitializeAsync`/load command.
- **What to test (arrange–act–assert)**
  - Commands: `CanExecute` true/false for given state; `Execute` changes state or calls the right service.
  - Property notifications: subscribe to `PropertyChanged` and assert the expected names were raised (including
    computed properties).
  - Validation: invalid input produces errors (`HasErrors`, `GetErrors`), valid input clears them.
  - Async flows: busy flag set and cleared, errors surfaced, cancellation honoured.
  - Messages: when using a messenger, a test can register as a recipient and assert the message was sent.
- **One behaviour per test,** and avoid asserting on exception message text.
pitfalls: ViewModels that call `MessageBox.Show` or `new SomeWindow()` — the test either blocks or needs a UI thread.
Using `Application.Current.Dispatcher` in a ViewModel — `Application.Current` is `null` in a test run.
`async void` command handlers that a test can't await, giving flaky assertions.
Testing private implementation details instead of the observable behaviour (state, notifications, service calls).
followUps: How would you test a ViewModel that uses a timer or the current time?
What is the difference between a fake, a stub and a mock?
How do you test code that marshals work to the UI thread?

questions.question: Why does WPF throw "The calling thread cannot access this object because a different thread owns it"? What is thread affinity?
questions.shortAnswer: Most WPF objects derive from `DispatcherObject`, which remembers the `Dispatcher` of the thread that created it; only that thread may use the object, and `VerifyAccess` throws an `InvalidOperationException` when another thread tries. Long work belongs on a background thread or an async API, and anything that touches UI objects must be marshalled back to the UI thread through its `Dispatcher` (or by awaiting from UI code).
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **One UI thread, one queue.** The UI thread processes work items from its `Dispatcher` queue one at a time, by
  priority. Keeping each item short keeps the app responsive.
- **Thread affinity:** a `DispatcherObject` stores the creating thread's `Dispatcher`; `CheckAccess()` returns
  `true`/`false`, `VerifyAccess()` throws if the caller is on a different thread.
- **Typical trigger:** a `Task.Run`, timer callback or event from a background service sets `textBox.Text`, adds to
  a bound `ObservableCollection`, or creates a brush that the UI later uses.
- **Fixes**
  - Do the slow part off the UI thread and `await` it from UI code — the code after `await` resumes on the UI
    thread.
  - From non-UI code, queue work with `Dispatcher.InvokeAsync`/`BeginInvoke` (asynchronous) or `Invoke`
    (synchronous).
  - Use `Progress<T>` for progress reports.
- **Freezables are the exception:** a *frozen* `Freezable` (brush, geometry, transform) can't be modified, so it
  can be shared across threads — freeze objects created on a background thread before handing them to the UI.
- **Multiple UI threads are possible** (a window on its own STA thread with its own dispatcher), but each window's
  elements still belong to their own thread.
pitfalls: Wrapping every UI update in `Dispatcher.Invoke` "just in case" instead of structuring code with `await`.
Creating brushes or bitmaps on a background thread and using them unfrozen on the UI thread.
Assuming `async` alone moves work off the UI thread — CPU-bound code before the first `await` still runs on the UI thread.
Blocking the UI thread with `Thread.Sleep` or long loops, which freezes rendering and input.
followUps: What is the difference between `Dispatcher.Invoke`, `BeginInvoke` and `InvokeAsync`?
Why can a frozen `Freezable` be shared across threads?
Can a WPF app have more than one UI thread? Why would you do it?

questions.question: What is the difference between `Dispatcher.Invoke`, `BeginInvoke` and `InvokeAsync`, and what does `DispatcherPriority` control?
questions.shortAnswer: All three queue a delegate on the UI thread's dispatcher. `Invoke` is synchronous — the caller blocks until the UI thread has run the delegate; `BeginInvoke` and `InvokeAsync` return immediately, and `InvokeAsync` (added in .NET Framework 4.5) returns a `DispatcherOperation` you can `await`. `DispatcherPriority` decides where in the queue the work goes relative to input, layout and rendering.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **`Invoke(action)`** — blocks the calling thread until the delegate completes; returns its result. Simple, but a
  background thread now waits on the UI thread.
- **`BeginInvoke(delegate, args)`** — older asynchronous API; returns a `DispatcherOperation`; fire-and-forget
  style.
- **`InvokeAsync(action or func, priority)`** — asynchronous, returns `DispatcherOperation`/`DispatcherOperation<T>`
  with a `Task`, so `await Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() => ...)` works naturally. Preferred in new code.
- **Priorities:** ten levels in `DispatcherPriority`, from `Send` (highest) through `Normal`, `Render`, `Loaded`,
  `Input`, `Background`, `ApplicationIdle` to `SystemIdle`. Queuing low-priority work (`Background`, `SystemIdle`)
  lets input and rendering run first — the docs use `SystemIdle` to chop a long calculation into small pieces on
  the UI thread.
- **When you're already on the UI thread**, just call the code; `Dispatcher.CheckAccess()` tells you.

**Deadlock risk with `Invoke`**

If the UI thread is itself blocked waiting for the background thread (for example `.Wait()` on a task, or a lock
held by the background thread), a synchronous `Invoke` from that background thread can never complete. The
asynchronous variants avoid that particular deadlock.
pitfalls: Calling `Dispatcher.Invoke` from a background thread while the UI thread waits on that thread — classic deadlock.
Flooding the dispatcher with thousands of tiny `InvokeAsync` calls (one per item) instead of batching updates.
Using `Send` priority for ordinary updates, starving input and rendering.
Grabbing `Application.Current.Dispatcher` inside ViewModels, which ties them to WPF and breaks in unit tests.
followUps: When would you deliberately queue work at `DispatcherPriority.Background` or `ApplicationIdle`?
How does `await` relate to the dispatcher in a WPF app?
How would you batch many updates coming from a background feed?
questions.versionNote: `Dispatcher.InvokeAsync` was added in .NET Framework 4.5 and is available in all WPF on .NET versions; older code typically uses `BeginInvoke` with a `Delegate`.

questions.question: How do `async`/`await` interact with the WPF UI thread? When do you use `Task.Run`, `ConfigureAwait(false)` and `Progress<T>`?
questions.shortAnswer: WPF installs a `DispatcherSynchronizationContext` on the UI thread, and `await` captures it by default, so code after an `await` in an event handler or ViewModel command resumes on the UI thread and can touch the UI. Use naturally async APIs for I/O, `Task.Run` only to move CPU-bound work off the UI thread, `ConfigureAwait(false)` in general-purpose library code that doesn't need the UI context, and `Progress<T>` to report progress back safely.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Context capture:** `await` remembers `SynchronizationContext.Current`; on the UI thread that posts the
  continuation back to the dispatcher.
- **I/O-bound work** (HTTP, database, files): call the `...Async` APIs directly — no thread is blocked while
  waiting, so `Task.Run` adds nothing.
- **CPU-bound work** (parsing, image processing, big calculations): `await Task.Run(() => Compute())` so the UI
  thread keeps pumping input and rendering.
- **`ConfigureAwait(false)`:** don't resume on the captured context. Recommended in reusable library code (fewer
  hops, no dependency on the UI); generally *not* needed in app-level UI code, where you usually want to come back
  to the UI thread. It doesn't guarantee a thread switch if the awaited task has already completed.
- **`Progress<T>`** captures the synchronization context when it is constructed and invokes its handler through
  it, so a background task can call `progress.Report(x)` and the handler runs on the UI thread.
- **Cancellation:** pass a `CancellationToken` from a "Cancel" command down through the async calls.
- **`BackgroundWorker`** is the legacy event-based option; `async`/`await` with `Task.Run` and `Progress<T>` covers
  the same needs more cleanly.
pitfalls: Wrapping I/O calls in `Task.Run` — it burns a pool thread for nothing.
Using `ConfigureAwait(false)` in a ViewModel and then touching bound properties or collections afterwards — you may no longer be on the UI thread.
Creating `Progress<T>` on a background thread, so its handler doesn't run on the UI thread.
Doing heavy CPU work before the first `await` in an async method, which still blocks the UI thread.
followUps: Why does `.Result` on an async method called from a button click freeze the app?
How would you cancel a long-running import and leave the UI in a consistent state?
When is `BackgroundWorker` still acceptable?

questions.question: Calling `LoadDataAsync().Result` from a button click freezes the app forever. Explain the deadlock and how to fix it.
questions.shortAnswer: `.Result` blocks the UI thread until the task finishes, but inside `LoadDataAsync` an `await` captured the UI `SynchronizationContext`, so its continuation is queued to run on the UI thread — which is blocked waiting for that very continuation. Neither can proceed. The fix is to stay asynchronous all the way up (`await` in an `async` handler or async command); `ConfigureAwait(false)` in library code reduces the risk but isn't a substitute.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Step by step**
  1. The click handler (UI thread) calls `LoadDataAsync()` and then `.Result`, blocking the UI thread.
  2. Inside, `await httpClient.GetStringAsync(...)` captures the UI context and returns an incomplete task.
  3. The download completes; its continuation is *posted* to the UI thread's dispatcher.
  4. The UI thread is blocked in `.Result`, so the continuation never runs, so the task never completes.
- **Same problem with** `.Wait()`, `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()`, `Task.WaitAll` and synchronous
  `Dispatcher.Invoke` from the awaited code.
- **Fixes, best first**
  - Async all the way: `private async void Load_Click(...) { Data = await LoadDataAsync(); }` (event handlers are
    the one place `async void` is expected), or an async command.
  - In reusable libraries, `ConfigureAwait(false)` on internal awaits so they don't need the UI thread.
  - If a synchronous API is unavoidable, run the async work on the thread pool
    (`Task.Run(() => LoadDataAsync()).GetAwaiter().GetResult()`) — still blocks the UI, so only for short,
    exceptional cases.
- **Symptoms:** the window stops repainting, no exception is thrown, and the debugger shows the UI thread waiting
  inside `Task.Wait`/`GetResult`.
pitfalls: Patching the freeze with `ConfigureAwait(false)` in one place while another `await` deeper in the call chain still captures the context.
Calling async code synchronously from a constructor or property getter — move loading into an explicit async method or command.
Using `async void` outside event handlers, so exceptions can't be caught by callers.
Calling `Dispatcher.Invoke` from code the UI thread is synchronously waiting on.
followUps: Why doesn't the same code deadlock in a console app?
How would you load data when a window opens without blocking its constructor?
Does `ConfigureAwait(false)` guarantee the continuation runs on a thread-pool thread?

questions.question: You add items to a bound `ObservableCollection<T>` from a background thread and get an exception. Why, and what are your options?
questions.shortAnswer: The `ItemsControl` and the `CollectionView` WPF wraps around your collection have affinity to the UI thread, and they react to `CollectionChanged` on whatever thread raises it — so changing the collection from another thread throws. Either marshal changes to the UI thread (await back, `Dispatcher.InvokeAsync`, ideally in batches) or call `BindingOperations.EnableCollectionSynchronization` with a lock and take that lock for every access.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Why:** WPF reads the collection through a `CollectionView`; both it and the items control belong to the UI
  thread, so the restriction effectively applies to the collection too.
- **Option 1 — marshal to the UI thread (most common)**
  - Do the slow work in the background, then add results after `await`, which resumes on the UI thread.
  - From a pure background callback, `Dispatcher.InvokeAsync(() => Items.Add(x))`.
  - Batch: build a `List<T>` in the background and swap it in (new collection or one bulk update) instead of
    thousands of individual `Add` calls.
- **Option 2 — `BindingOperations.EnableCollectionSynchronization(collection, lockObject)`**
  (.NET Framework 4.5+)
  - Call it on the UI thread, before the collection is used from another thread or attached to the control.
  - Every access by your code must take the same lock; changes and their notifications must be atomic
    (`ObservableCollection<T>` is, as long as you lock).
  - WPF keeps a shadow copy and applies queued change events on the UI thread when it can, throttled so a busy
    producer can't starve user input.
  - A callback overload supports other synchronization mechanisms.
- **Scalar properties** raised via `INotifyPropertyChanged` from a background thread are a separate topic; many
  teams simply keep all ViewModel mutations on the UI thread to avoid surprises.
pitfalls: Calling `EnableCollectionSynchronization` from a background thread or after background updates have already started.
Locking in your writer but reading or enumerating the collection elsewhere without the lock.
Marshalling every single item with `Dispatcher.Invoke` — slow, and synchronous calls risk deadlocks.
Replacing the collection instance from a background thread — the property change and the new collection still need the UI thread.
followUps: How would you display a high-rate log stream without freezing the UI?
What does the "shadow copy" in `EnableCollectionSynchronization` imply about what the UI shows at a given instant?
How do you add many items to an `ObservableCollection` efficiently?
questions.versionNote: `BindingOperations.EnableCollectionSynchronization` exists from .NET Framework 4.5 onwards and in all WPF on .NET versions; on .NET Framework 4.0 and earlier, marshalling every change to the UI thread was the only option.

questions.question: How do you implement global exception handling in a WPF app? Which events catch which exceptions?
questions.shortAnswer: Handle `Application.DispatcherUnhandledException` for exceptions thrown on the main UI thread — log, show a friendly message and set `e.Handled = true` if the app can safely continue; add `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException` to log exceptions from other threads before the process terminates; and `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` for faulted tasks nobody awaited. Exceptions on background threads never reach `DispatcherUnhandledException` on their own.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **`Application.DispatcherUnhandledException`**
  - Raised for each unhandled exception in code running on the *main UI thread* (event handlers, commands,
    continuations after `await` in UI code).
  - Set `e.Handled = true` to stop WPF's default behaviour (error dialog and shutdown) — only when the error is
    recoverable; a `StackOverflowException` is not.
  - There is no `OnDispatcherUnhandledException` override; you must subscribe to the event.
- **Other threads:** exceptions on a background UI thread or a worker thread are *not* forwarded. Catch them there,
  or marshal them to the UI thread and rethrow, so the global handler sees them.
- **`AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException`** — last-chance notification for any thread; lets you log or save
  data, but the process still terminates (`IsTerminating`). Not raised for corrupted-state exceptions such as stack
  overflows.
- **`TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException`** — a faulted task whose exception was never observed; raised when the
  task is finalized. By default (since .NET Framework 4.5) it no longer terminates the process. Call `SetObserved()`
  after logging.
- **Prefer local handling:** catch expected failures where they happen (service calls in commands) and surface them
  in the UI; the global handlers are a safety net, not error handling.
pitfalls: Setting `Handled = true` for every exception, leaving the app running in a corrupted state.
Expecting `DispatcherUnhandledException` to catch exceptions thrown inside `Task.Run` or a `System.Threading.Timer` callback.
Throwing again (or showing modal dialogs in a loop) from inside the global handler.
Relying on the global handler instead of catching expected errors in `async void` handlers and commands.
followUps: How would you report exceptions from a background service to the user?
What is the WinForms equivalent of `DispatcherUnhandledException`?
When should the app shut down instead of continuing after an exception?
questions.versionNote: Since .NET Framework 4.5 (and in .NET Core/.NET), unobserved task exceptions don't terminate the process by default; on .NET Framework 4.0 they did, and `<ThrowUnobservedTaskExceptions enabled="true"/>` restores that behaviour on .NET Framework.

questions.question: What are the main differences between Windows Forms and WPF, and how would you choose between them for a new desktop app?
questions.shortAnswer: Windows Forms is a mature, designer-first, event-driven framework built around Win32 controls and pixel-based layout; WPF describes UI in XAML, renders with a resolution-independent, hardware-accelerated vector engine, and is built around data binding, templates and styles. Both are Windows-only, open source and supported on modern .NET; pick WinForms for fast, simple forms-over-data tools and legacy code, and WPF for rich, restyled or data-heavy UIs and MVVM-style architecture.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
| | Windows Forms | WPF |
|---|---|---|
| UI definition | Visual designer generating C# (`InitializeComponent` in `*.Designer.cs`) | XAML markup + code-behind |
| Rendering | Win32 controls; custom drawing with `System.Drawing` | Vector-based, resolution-independent engine using graphics hardware |
| Units | Pixels (with DPI scaling modes) | Device-independent pixels (1/96 inch) |
| Layout | `Location`/`Size`, `Anchor`, `Dock`, `TableLayoutPanel`, `FlowLayoutPanel` | Measure/arrange panels: `Grid`, `StackPanel`, `DockPanel`… |
| Customisation | Properties, owner-draw, custom controls | Styles, control templates, data templates, triggers, animation |
| Data binding | `DataBindings`, `BindingSource`; WPF-like command binding since .NET 8 | Central to the framework (`DataContext`, binding modes, converters, validation) |
| Typical architecture | Event handlers in the form (MVP/MVVM possible) | MVVM |

- **Both** have a .NET Framework 4.x implementation (part of Windows) and an open-source implementation on modern
  .NET; neither runs on macOS/Linux.
- **Choose WinForms** for internal line-of-business tools, quick data-entry screens, or extending an existing
  WinForms codebase.
- **Choose WPF** when you need custom visuals, theming, complex data presentation, high-DPI fidelity, or a testable
  MVVM structure.
- **Mixing is possible:** `WindowsFormsHost` and `ElementHost` let each host the other's controls during a gradual
  migration.
pitfalls: Saying WinForms is "obsolete" or ".NET Framework only" — it is supported and actively developed on modern .NET.
Assuming WPF runs cross-platform because modern .NET does.
Porting WinForms habits (absolute positioning, logic in click handlers) into WPF and losing its layout and binding benefits.
Ignoring DPI behaviour when choosing — WPF's device-independent units scale naturally; WinForms needs its DPI mode configured.
followUps: How would you migrate a large WinForms app to WPF incrementally?
How does WPF achieve resolution independence?
What changed in WinForms data binding in .NET 7 and 8?

questions.question: In Windows Forms, what is the difference between `Anchor` and `Dock`? Why does the order of docked controls matter?
questions.shortAnswer: `Anchor` keeps a control at a fixed distance from the parent edges you pick (anchor left *and* right and it stretches horizontally); `Dock` glues a control to one edge — or `Fill` — and lets the parent size and position it. The two are mutually exclusive (the last one set wins), and docked controls are laid out in z-order, so the order in the `Controls` collection decides who gets the full width or height.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Anchor** (`AnchorStyles`, default `Top | Left`)
  - The control keeps its distance to each anchored edge as the container resizes.
  - Anchoring opposite edges (`Left | Right`) makes it stretch; anchoring only `Bottom | Right` makes it move.
- **Dock** (`DockStyle`: `None`, `Top`, `Bottom`, `Left`, `Right`, `Fill`)
  - The container decides size and position: docked `Top` keeps its height but takes the available width; docked
    `Left` keeps its width.
  - You can't set `Location` on a docked control, and its `Margin` doesn't change its distance from the edges.
- **Docking order = z-order.** Controls are docked in z-order; whichever docks first takes the full length of its
  edge. If two controls dock to the same side they stack. In the designer, *Bring to Front* / *Send to Back*
  changes the order — the `Fill` control should be docked last so it takes only the remaining space.
- **Mutually exclusive:** setting `Dock` clears the effect of `Anchor` and vice versa.
- **Bigger layouts:** `TableLayoutPanel` (rows and columns that resize proportionally) and `FlowLayoutPanel`
  (wrapping flow) avoid hand-tuned anchors; `SplitContainer` adds a resizable splitter.
pitfalls: A `Fill` panel hiding under a toolbar because it was docked before the toolbar — fix the z-order (Bring to Front).
Setting both `Dock` and `Anchor` and expecting both to apply — only the last one set takes effect.
Using `Margin` to push a docked control away from the edge — use the container's `Padding` instead.
Hand-positioning every control and then fighting DPI or localisation changes; layout panels adapt better.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Form.Show()` and `Form.ShowDialog()`? How do you return a result from a dialog, and who disposes it?
questions.shortAnswer: `ShowDialog()` opens the form modally: the calling code stops until the dialog closes and gets back a `DialogResult`; `Show()` opens a modeless window and returns immediately. Closing a modal dialog only hides it, so you must dispose it yourself (a `using` block is the usual pattern), whereas a modeless form shown with `Show()` is disposed when it is closed.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Modal (`ShowDialog`)**
  - Blocks the code after the call (the message loop keeps running for the dialog) and disables input to the owner.
  - Returns a `DialogResult`, set by a button's `DialogResult` property or by assigning `this.DialogResult` in code
    (which also closes the dialog).
  - Clicking the X sets `DialogResult.Cancel`.
  - The form is **hidden, not disposed**, so it can be shown again — call `Dispose()` when you are done.
  - `ShowDialog(this)` sets the owner explicitly; without it the currently active window becomes the owner.
- **Modeless (`Show`)**
  - Returns immediately; both windows stay interactive.
  - Communicate results through events, properties or a callback; the form disposes itself when closed.
- **Reading results:** expose properties on the dialog (`SelectedCustomer`) and read them *before* disposing.
- **Validation:** cancel closing (`FormClosing` with `e.Cancel = true`, or reset `DialogResult = DialogResult.None`)
  when input is invalid.
pitfalls: Forgetting to dispose forms shown with `ShowDialog` — each one leaks its window handle and controls until finalised.
Reading control values after disposing the dialog.
Calling `ShowDialog` on a form that is already visible, which throws `InvalidOperationException`.
Showing a dialog without an owner from background code, so it appears behind the main window.
followUps: How do `AcceptButton` and `CancelButton` relate to `DialogResult`?

questions.question: Why does WinForms throw "Cross-thread operation not valid", and what are the correct ways to update a control from background work?
questions.shortAnswer: WinForms controls must be created and used on the thread that owns their window (the UI thread); touching them from another thread is unsafe, and under the debugger it reliably throws `InvalidOperationException` ("Control accessed from a thread other than the thread it was created on"). Do background work with `async`/`await` (plus `Task.Run` for CPU work) so updates happen back on the UI thread, or marshal explicitly with `Control.Invoke`/`BeginInvoke`, or `Control.InvokeAsync` on .NET 9+.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Why:** Windows delivers a window's messages to the thread that created it; controls aren't thread-safe, so
  other threads must ask the UI thread to do the work.
- **Detection:** `Control.CheckForIllegalCrossThreadCalls` makes the debugger throw; turning it off hides the bug
  but doesn't fix it.
- **Options**
  - **`async`/`await`** in event handlers: await I/O directly or `await Task.Run(...)` for CPU work; code after
    `await` resumes on the UI thread (WinForms installs a `WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext`).
  - **`InvokeRequired` + `Invoke`** — synchronous marshal; the calling thread waits for the UI thread.
  - **`BeginInvoke`** — asynchronous marshal, fire-and-forget.
  - **`Control.InvokeAsync`** (.NET 9+) — posts to the UI thread and returns an awaitable `Task`, supports
    cancellation and async delegates, and avoids common `Invoke` deadlocks.
  - **`BackgroundWorker`** — legacy event model (`DoWork`, `ProgressChanged`, `RunWorkerCompleted`); still
    supported but no longer recommended.
- **Progress:** `IProgress<T>`/`Progress<T>` created on the UI thread reports safely.
- **Deadlock warning:** `Invoke` from a worker while the UI thread waits on that worker (`.Wait()`, `.Result`)
  freezes both.
pitfalls: Setting `CheckForIllegalCrossThreadCalls = false` to silence the exception.
Using synchronous `Invoke` for every message from a busy background thread — it serialises the worker behind the UI.
Blocking the UI thread with `.Result`/`.Wait()` while a worker calls `Invoke`, causing a deadlock.
Calling `Invoke` before the control's handle exists (in the constructor) or after the form is disposed.
followUps: What does `InvokeRequired` actually compare?
How does `Control.InvokeAsync` differ from `BeginInvoke`?
What is the WinForms equivalent of WPF's `Dispatcher`?

questions.question: Why doesn't a `DataGridView` refresh when you add items to the `List<T>` it is bound to? Explain `BindingList<T>`, `INotifyPropertyChanged` and `BindingSource`.
questions.shortAnswer: `List<T>` raises no change notifications, so the grid never learns that items were added or removed (and can even try to paint rows that no longer exist). `BindingList<T>` implements `IBindingList` and raises `ListChanged` for list changes — and for item changes when the items implement `INotifyPropertyChanged` — while a `BindingSource` sits between data and controls to provide currency (the current row), change notification and extras such as binding to plain `IEnumerable`s.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **Two kinds of binding**
  - *Simple*: one property to one value — `textBox.DataBindings.Add("Text", customer, "Name")`.
  - *Complex (list-based)*: `DataGridView`, `ListBox`, `ComboBox` via `DataSource`.
- **Lists need `IList`; notifications need `IBindingList`.** `List<T>` is bindable but silent; `BindingList<T>` is
  the generic `IBindingList` implementation recommended for business objects.
- **Item changes:** items should implement `INotifyPropertyChanged`; `BindingList<T>` turns `PropertyChanged` into
  `ListChanged` (`ItemChanged`) so the grid repaints that row.
- **`BindingSource`** — the usual intermediary: bind controls to it and it to the data.
  - Tracks the current item (`Current`, `Position`, `MoveNext()`), so a grid and detail text boxes stay in sync.
  - Lets list controls bind to `IEnumerable` sources (it copies them into a list).
  - `ResetBindings(false)` forces a refresh when the source can't notify.
- **Edits and rollback:** `IEditableObject` (`BeginEdit`/`EndEdit`/`CancelEdit`) is used by `DataGridView` for
  row-level cancel.

**Detail**

Resetting `DataSource = null` and re-assigning it works as a workaround but loses the current position and
selection; switching the source to a `BindingList<T>` (optionally behind a `BindingSource`) fixes the cause.
pitfalls: Binding a `List<T>`, then calling `Clear()` or `Add()` and getting a stale grid or `IndexOutOfRangeException` while painting.
Implementing `INotifyPropertyChanged` on items but keeping them in a `List<T>` — item edits still don't reach the grid reliably.
Binding the grid and the detail controls to the list directly instead of the same `BindingSource`, so they don't share the current row.
Modifying a bound `BindingList<T>` from a background thread.

questions.question: Can you use MVVM in Windows Forms? What did .NET 7 and .NET 8 add for command and data binding?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes — and on modern .NET it is directly supported: Windows Forms on .NET 8 fully enables a newer, WPF-inspired data binding engine (previewed in .NET 7), `Control.DataContext` (an ambient property, .NET 7+), and `ButtonBase.Command`/`CommandParameter`, so a button can bind to an `ICommand` and enables or disables itself from `CanExecute`. That lets you share ViewModels (for example written with CommunityToolkit.Mvvm) between WinForms, WPF, WinUI and .NET MAUI, although WinForms still has no XAML.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **What's new**
  - A binding engine modelled after WPF, driven by `IBindableComponent`/`BindableComponent`, which `Control`
    implements — designed to make MVVM practical and reduce code-behind.
  - `ButtonBase.Command` and `CommandParameter`: clicking invokes the command; the button listens to
    `CanExecuteChanged` and enables itself when `CanExecute` returns `true`. Settable in the designer under
    **(DataBindings)**.
  - `Control.DataContext` (since .NET 7): an ambient data context that child controls inherit, with
    `DataContextChanged` for controls (often via a `BindingSource`) to pick it up.
- **What it enables:** ViewModels with `INotifyPropertyChanged` properties and `ICommand`s, unit-tested without
  UI, reused across .NET UI frameworks; forms shrink to binding setup.
- **What it is not:** there's no XAML, templating or styling system — layout and visuals are still the designer and
  controls.
- **On .NET Framework** you can still apply MVVM or MVP by hand (`DataBindings`, `BindingSource`,
  `INotifyPropertyChanged`, wiring `Click` to commands manually), but without `Command` properties.
pitfalls: Claiming WinForms "can't do MVVM" — on .NET 8+ commands and WPF-style binding are built in.
Expecting XAML-style templates or styles to come with the binding engine.
Targeting .NET Framework and looking for `Button.Command` — it doesn't exist there.
Updating ViewModel properties from background threads; bound WinForms controls still need the UI thread.
followUps: How would you structure a WinForms app so most logic lives in testable ViewModels?

questions.question: How do you host a Windows Forms control inside WPF, or a WPF control inside Windows Forms, and what limitations should you expect?
questions.shortAnswer: The `System.Windows.Forms.Integration` namespace provides `WindowsFormsHost`, a WPF element that hosts a WinForms control, and `ElementHost`, a WinForms control that hosts a WPF element. They make gradual migrations and reuse of legacy controls possible, but each hosted control is a separate HWND: it always draws on top of WPF content ("airspace"), can't be rotated or skewed, scales and goes transparent only partially, and nesting more than one level of hybrid controls isn't supported.
questions.answer:
**Key points**
- **WinForms in WPF — `WindowsFormsHost`:** declare it in XAML (or code) and set its `Child`; it maps ambient
  properties (font, colours) to the WinForms control and coordinates tabbing and keyboard focus.
- **WPF in WinForms — `ElementHost`:** set its `Child` to any WPF `UIElement` (a `UserControl` is typical); for a
  modeless WPF window opened from WinForms, call `ElementHost.EnableModelessKeyboardInterop(window)` so keyboard
  input works.
- **Limitations**
  - Hosted WinForms controls always render above WPF elements — WPF z-order and overlap don't apply.
  - No rotation/skew via WPF transforms; proportional scaling depends on the control.
  - Transparency is partial (`TextBox`, `ComboBox` aren't transparent).
  - Some controls have fixed sizes (a WinForms `ComboBox` height).
  - Shortcut keys handled by WinForms pre-processing win over WPF commands bound to the same keys.
  - Multilevel hybrids (WinForms → WPF → WinForms) are not supported.
  - Both sides are still single-threaded UI.
- **Use it for:** migrating screen by screen, reusing a third-party WinForms control (grid, chart, report viewer)
  in a WPF app, or adding a modern WPF view into a legacy WinForms shell.

code.source:
<!-- WPF window hosting a legacy WinForms DataGridView -->
<Window x:Class="Shell.MainWindow"
        xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation"
        xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"
        xmlns:wf="clr-namespace:System.Windows.Forms;assembly=System.Windows.Forms">
    <DockPanel>
        <TextBlock DockPanel.Dock="Top" Text="Orders (legacy grid)" Margin="8" />
        <WindowsFormsHost>
            <wf:DataGridView x:Name="legacyGrid" AutoSizeColumnsMode="Fill" />
        </WindowsFormsHost>
    </DockPanel>
</Window>

<!-- The reverse, in a WinForms form (C#):
     var host = new System.Windows.Forms.Integration.ElementHost { Dock = DockStyle.Fill };
     host.Child = new Dashboard.ChartView();   // a WPF UserControl
     Controls.Add(host); -->

pitfalls: Placing WPF popups, adorners or overlays on top of a `WindowsFormsHost` and finding they are hidden behind it.
Applying a WPF `RenderTransform`/animation to a hosted WinForms control and expecting it to rotate or fade.
Nesting WPF inside WinForms inside WPF — multilevel hybrids aren't supported.
Forgetting `EnableModelessKeyboardInterop` for a modeless WPF window opened from WinForms, so keys don't reach it.
